Probe-Geometry Alignment:
Erasing the Cross-Sequence Memorization Signature Below Chance Thanks: Preprint. Under review at NeurIPS 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/Rupawheatly/MLDU.

Anamika Paul Rupa Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Affiliation: Howard University Affiliation: Washington, DC, USA Email: anamikal.rupa@howard.edu    Anietie Andy Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Affiliation: Howard University Affiliation: Washington, DC, USA Email: anietie.andy@howard.edu
Abstract

Recent attacks show that behavioural unlearning of large language models leaves internal traces recoverable by adversarial probes [1, 2, 3, 4]. We characterise where this retention lives and show it can be surgically removed without measurable capability cost. Our central protocol is a leave-one-out cross-sequence probe that tests whether a memorisation signature generalises across held-out sequences. The signature is real and consistent across scale: memorisation-specific gaps of +0.32+0.32, +0.19+0.19, +0.30+0.30 on Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, and Mistral-7B against a random-initialisation control on the same architecture, where the deep-layer gap collapses to −0.04-0.04 at the network’s deepest layer (L6 of Pythia-70M, where the pretrained signature peaks). The probe direction is causally separable from recall — projecting it out collapses the signature locally (+→−0.19+0.44\!\to\!-0.19) while behavioural recall barely changes — and a probe trained on naturally memorised content does not classify fine-tuning-injected secrets as memorised, marking two representationally distinct regimes. We then introduce probe-geometry alignment (PGA), a surgical erasure that aligns activations along the probe’s live readout direction at each depth (one scalar per depth, not the full residual). PGA drives the cross-sequence probe below random chance at all four scales tested (toy: depth-44 0.170.17; Pythia-70M 0.070.07; Mistral-7B 0.450.45; GPT-2 medium 0.060.06 via MD-PGA k=2k\!=\!2) and remains robust to six adversarial probe variants. Against a stronger threat — a re-fitting attacker who trains a fresh probe on PGA-treated activations — we extend PGA adversarially (iterative orthogonal subspace augmentation), defeating the re-fit probe at every memorisation-relevant depth while preserving five zero-shot capability benchmarks (HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ, ARC-Easy, WinoGrande) within 2.82.8 percentage points per task (max |Δ​acc|=2.8|\Delta\mathrm{acc}|\!=\!2.8pp on BoolQ; mean Δ​acc=+0.2\Delta\mathrm{acc}\!=\!+0.2pp). The cross-sequence signature is a real, causally separable, regime-specific property of pretrained representations — removable below chance with a single rank-one intervention per depth at no measurable capability cost.

   

August 24, 2026

1 Introduction

Machine unlearning for large language models has a measurement problem. Every major evaluation framework — TOFU [5], MUSE [6], WMDP [7] — assesses whether a model still generates the target content. None assess whether the model still encodes it internally. We show these are different questions with different answers, using a probe protocol whose validity does not depend on the saturated within-sequence behaviour it replaces.

Why this matters.

The stakes for unlearning are real. Regulatory frameworks and legal pressures — including GDPR’s Right to be Forgotten and increasing copyright litigation — mandate removal of personal data and copyrighted material from trained models. Model developers must remove trade secrets, proprietary datasets, and unsafe content discovered post-deployment [8, 7]. Concurrent attacks show that a model can behaviorally suppress a memorized secret — stopping generation on command — yet leave sufficient internal trace that adversarial probes extract it [1, 2]. If unlearning is only behavioral, it is compliance theater: the information is still there, just silent. This paper measures whether the information is actually gone from the model’s internal representations, not merely hidden from the output.

The cross-sequence signature.

Our central empirical finding is that naturally memorized content produces a cross-sequence linear signature that generalizes via leave-one-out (LOO): a probe trained on memorized/non-memorized activation pairs for some sequences classifies a held-out sequence at high accuracy. The memorization-specific gap (true LOO minus pure-distinguishability baseline) is +0.32+0.32 on Pythia-70M, +0.19+0.19 on GPT-2 medium, and +0.30+0.30 on Mistral-7B (Fig. 6), against a random-initialization control on the same architecture: while random-init Pythia retains some cross-sequence structure in shallow layers (mean transformer-layer gap +0.19+0.19, dominated by L0/L1 token-identity propagation through random transformations), this baseline collapses to −0.04-0.04 at L6 — the deepest layer, where the pretrained signature peaks. The pretraining-attributable signature thus lives in deep layers where random-init has essentially no structure. The signature is cluster-specific (strong for formal-register English and licenses, near-null for code and pseudo-Latin) and a probe trained on natural memorization does not recognize fine-tuning-injected secrets (Section 5.5) — two representationally distinct memorization regimes.

Toy verification and a constructive follow-up.

Section 4 mechanistically verifies the dissociation in a controlled toy transformer where causal attribution is unambiguous (single dominant attention head, normalised causal effect =1.000=1.000). The toy also surfaces the measurement problem motivating LOO probing: single-sequence probes saturate at 1.0001.000 by construction (Section 3.1), so they cannot reveal whether unlearning has actually changed internal structure. Building on the dissociation finding, we introduce probe-geometry alignment (PGA), a surgical erasure that aligns activations along the probe’s live readout direction at each depth. PGA collapses the cross-sequence probe (→0.651.00\!\to\!0.65 on the toy, deep depths below random chance), preserves PPL, holds against six adversarial probe variants, and scales across four architectures spanning four orders of magnitude (0.80.8M toy →\to Mistral-7B). Whether the probe-detected structure is exploitable for adversarial token extraction at scale [9] remains a separate open question.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    Cross-sequence LOO probing protocol (§3). A leave-one-out probe testing whether the memorisation signature generalises across held-out sequences — distinguishing genuine signature from model-level shifts [1] or representational drift [2]. Validated on Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, and Mistral-7B: memorisation-specific gaps of +0.32+0.32, +0.19+0.19, +0.30+0.30 against a random-initialization null of +0.19+0.19.

  2. 2.

    Causal separability of the probe direction (§3.5). Projecting the fitted probe direction out of the residual stream collapses the signature locally (+→−0.19+0.44\!\to\!-0.19) yet behavioural recall barely changes (≤0.19\leq\!0.19 nats drop). The probe-readable structure and the recall-producing structure occupy separable directions.

  3. 3.

    Two memorisation regimes with distinct signatures (§5.5). A probe trained on naturally memorised sequences does not classify fine-tuning-injected secrets as memorised. Pretraining memorisation and rapid fine-tuning memorisation leave representationally distinct traces.

  4. 4.

    Probe-geometry alignment (PGA), a surgical erasure (§7). PGA drives the cross-sequence probe below random chance at all four scales tested (0.650.65 toy / depth-44: 0.170.17; 0.070.07 Pythia-70M; 0.450.45 Mistral-7B; 0.060.06 GPT-2 medium via MD-PGA k=2k\!=\!2), robust to six adversarial probe variants. PGA acts as a one-scalar-per-depth alignment along the probe’s readout direction, in contrast to feature-matching distillation [10], concept-erasure projection [11], and gradient-reversal alignment [12], which act in dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}-D. We extend PGA adversarially (iterative orthogonal subspace augmentation) to defeat re-fitting attacker probes at every memorisation-relevant depth while preserving five zero-shot capability benchmarks within 2.82.8pp per task (mean Δ​acc=+0.2\Delta\mathrm{acc}\!=\!+0.2pp).

2 Background

Machine unlearning.

Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data without retraining the model from scratch [13]. For language models the standard recipes range from gradient scrubbing [14] and character-level surgical replacement [15] to gradient-orthogonal preference updates such as NPO [16], with surveys [17] cataloguing dozens of variants. The dominant evaluation framework, TOFU [5], asks whether the model still generates the target sequence; by this metric most methods succeed. The success is fragile, however: a benign downstream fine-tuning resurrects forgotten content [3, 18, 19], post-hoc quantisation alone reverses the effect of unlearning [4], and behavioural suppression does not generalise to paraphrased or semantically adjacent prompts [20]; broader surveys reach similar conclusions [21, 22]. All of these results infer representational retention indirectly — by exhibiting a robustness failure — and leave the locus of retention unspecified. Our work measures retention directly via cross-sequence linear probes on the residual stream and identifies the depths and directions that carry it.

Behaviour vs. representation, and causal tracing.

The distinction between behavioural removal (the model stops emitting the target) and representational removal (the model stops encoding it) is well established. Linear probes lower-bound the information a hidden state carries about a class [23, 24]; if a probe still classifies post-unlearning, the relevant structure is still there. Knowledge editing [25, 26] and activation steering [27] demonstrate that facts are distributed across many parameters and depths, so an edit applied at one head or layer can leave upstream storage intact. We use causal tracing [25] to identify the minimal circuit [28] that produces the secret completion, and use the cross-sequence probe to test whether erasure has reached that storage rather than merely silencing the output.

Positioning relative to concurrent work.

Two recent papers report directly that internal representations carry traces of unlearned content. Chen et al. [1] extract spectral fingerprints from principal activation directions and use them to classify unlearned models with high accuracy. Xu et al. [2] quantify representational drift of an unlearned model relative to its pre-unlearning version via PCA, CKA, and Fisher information, taxonomising reversible from irreversible forgetting. We share the central observation that behavioural suppression does not erase representations, and we extend it along four axes that neither prior work covers: (i) a leave-one-out probe that tests cross-sequence generalisation of the signature — rather than model-level fingerprinting — validated on Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, and Mistral-7B; (ii) direct evidence that the probe direction is causally separable from recall (projecting it out collapses the signature locally yet recall barely changes, §3.5); (iii) a regime distinction between naturally pretrained memorisation and fine-tuning-injected secrets, which leave representationally distinct traces (§5.5); and (iv) a constructive surgical erasure (PGA, §7) that drives the cross-sequence probe below random chance at all four scales. Concurrent attack papers [3, 20, 4] establish that retained content exists by exhibiting attacks; we localise where it lives in the residual stream and remove it.

3 Cross-Sequence Signature Across Three Pretrained Architectures

We introduce a leave-one-out (LOO) cross-sequence probing protocol (Section 3.1) and apply it to naturally memorized content in three pretrained architectures spanning two orders of magnitude: Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium (345M), and Mistral-7B (7.24B). A memorization-specific gap generalizes across held-out sequences in every model tested. Mechanistic toy verification (which motivates the LOO protocol) follows in Section 4. Setups and extended results: Appendices M, D, C.

3.1 Leave-One-Out Cross-Sequence Probe Protocol

The cross-sequence probing protocol (henceforth LOO) tests whether a memorization signature generalizes across held-out sequences.

Motivation: beyond single-sequence saturation.

Single-sequence probes saturate at accuracy 1.0001.000 and cannot distinguish memorization-specific structure from mere string identity. The LOO protocol corrects this by requiring a probe to generalize across distinct sequences: a model whose activations contain a cross-sequence memorization signature should produce activations where held-out memorized sequences pattern-match with memorized training sequences, even though their token content differs. This tests whether the signature is replicable structure rather than tied to specific tokens.

Here’s the intuition with a concrete example. Suppose a model memorizes two unrelated strings: the Apache 2.0 license preamble and the MIT license preamble. Both are formal legal text, both frequently appear in training data, yet they differ entirely in content and tokens. If memorization leaves a replicable signature (not just position ii encodes character cc), then the residual-stream activations for “Apache detected” and “MIT detected” should share a structure, allowing a probe trained on Apache activations to recognize MIT activations as “memorized,” even having never seen MIT during training. Conversely, if unlearning truly erases memorization, a held-out sequence from a memorized cluster should produce activations that fool the probe. Within-sequence saturation cannot distinguish these regimes because activations tied to specific tokens will always allow perfect reconstruction; cross-sequence generalization isolates a learnable why from the trivial that.

Procedure.

For each model we construct three pools:

  • •

    Memorized pool ℳ\mathcal{M}: NN sequences that pass per-model log-probability screening (log⁡P/tok>θM\log P/\text{tok}>\theta_{M}).

  • •

    Control pool 𝒞\mathcal{C}: for each s∈ℳs\in\mathcal{M}, a distractor sequence sharing the same prefix but with a randomly resampled completion of matched length.

  • •

    Neutral context pool ℬ\mathcal{B}: 24 short neutral prefixes (e.g., “Here is a passage: ”) which supply within-class variance.

For each s∈ℳs\in\mathcal{M} and each b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}, we extract the last-token residual stream activation at every depth dd of the transformer, producing a tensor of shape (|ℳ|,|ℬ|,D,dmodel)(|\mathcal{M}|,|\mathcal{B}|,D,d_{\text{model}}) for the positive class and the analogous tensor for the matched control.

LOO classifier.

For each depth dd and each held-out sequence sj∈ℳs_{j}\in\mathcal{M}, we fit a logistic regression probe on all (s,b)(s,b) activations for s∈ℳ∖{sj}s\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\{s_{j}\} (positive label 1 for memorized, 0 for matched control), then evaluate on (sj,b)(s_{j},b) activations for b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}. We report per-sequence accuracy and the mean across held-out sequences as “true LOO”.

Null baselines.

  • •

    Shuffled LOO. Identical procedure, but training labels are randomly permuted within each fold. Expected value 0.50.5 under the null hypothesis of no linear separability.

  • •

    Pure-distinguishability LOO. Identical procedure on a second set of sequences that do not pass the memorization screening threshold on the base model. This measures how much of the true LOO score comes from string-separability structure shared across non-memorized sequences.

The memorization-specific gap is defined as Δmem​(d)=true LOO​(d)−pure LOO​(d)\Delta_{\text{mem}}(d)=\text{true LOO}(d)-\text{pure LOO}(d). A positive gap indicates cross-sequence structure specific to memorization rather than to string features shared by the memorized pool’s prefixes.
