Variance notes.

Per-sequence LOO accuracy is evaluated over |ℬ|=24|\mathcal{B}|=24 test points and takes values in {0,1/24,2/24,…,1}\{0,1/24,2/24,\ldots,1\}; the standard error on a single cell is therefore non-trivial. We report per-depth means (averaged across held-out sequences) and averages across transformer layers. Full depth-by-depth heatmaps and per-sequence tables: Section 3.1.

3.2 Pythia-70M (70M parameters, GPT-NeoX)

We apply the LOO protocol to base-pretrained Pythia-70M. On the Pile corpus, 7/97/9 sequences pass log⁡P/tok>−2.0\log P/\text{tok}>-2.0; LOO across the 66 transformer-layer depths yields a memorization-specific gap of +0.32+0.32 (peak +0.554+0.554). Re-running with 55 different random seeds on an expanded 8-sequence pool gives +0.380+0.380, with seed-to-seed standard deviation below 0.0010.001 — essentially deterministic w.r.t. probe randomness. A randomly-initialized null on the same architecture has mean transformer-layer gap +0.19+0.19 (peak +0.33+0.33 at L1), but per-depth analysis reveals the random-init gap is concentrated in shallow layers (likely L0 token-identity leakage propagating through random transformations) and collapses to −0.04-0.04 at L6, the deepest layer where the pretrained signature peaks. The deep-layer pretraining-attributable signature is therefore real and substantial [29]. A surgical-unlearning feasibility sweep on naturally memorized content fails the joint criterion (Appendix O; scope qualifier, not a general claim). The parallel injected-secret experiment (which applies the MLDU pipeline of Section 4 to Pythia-70M) is reported in Appendix L.

Finding 1.

On base pretrained Pythia-70M, LOO probing yields a cross-sequence gap of +0.32+0.32 (77-seq) to +0.380+0.380 on an expanded 8-sequence pool (seed-to-seed std <0.001<\!0.001 across 5 probe seeds); randomly-initialized null gives mean gap +0.19+0.19. Surgical unlearning of naturally memorized content fails a joint feasibility criterion at this scale — a scope qualifier, not a general claim against unlearning.

3.3 GPT-2 Medium (345M parameters)

We screen GPT-2 medium [30] for naturally memorized sequences [31, 8]; the primary one is the Apache License 2.0 preamble (log⁡P=−0.116\log P=-0.116). The parallel injected-secret experiment (which applies the MLDU pipeline of Section 4 to this naturally memorized sequence) is reported in Appendix L.

Cross-sequence LOO with robustness.

7/97/9 sequences pass the threshold; LOO across 2525 depths yields mean transformer-layer gap +0.19+0.19 (peak L21: +0.45+0.45). The signature is stable under three independent robustness checks: (i) re-running the LOO probe with 5 different random seeds gives seed-to-seed standard deviation below 0.0010.001; (ii) bootstrapping the neutral-context pool with 100 replicates yields a 95%95\% confidence interval of [+0.184,+0.196][+0.184,+0.196] around the gap; and (iii) a 7-fold sequence jackknife (drop one of the seven memorised sequences and re-run the whole pipeline) produces seven gaps that are all strictly positive, with values spanning the interval [+0.095,+0.250][+0.095,+0.250] — so no single sequence drives the effect. Cluster-specific: strong for legal/license (0.980.98) and web boilerplate (1.001.00); at chance for code (0.500.50) and pseudo-Latin (0.500.50). A single-seed register-vs-memorization control (Appendix 3.7) further shows that the peak-gap-layer signature is not explained by formal-register effects: applied to 1919 register-matched but unmemorized legalese passages, the L21 probe classifies only 14.9%14.9\% as memorized (vs. 93.9%93.9\% at the embedding layer L0). Full numbers: Appendix D, 3.7, 3.7.

Finding 2.

On GPT-2 medium (345M), LOO cross-sequence probing yields 20/2420/24 strictly positive gaps across transformer layers (mean L11–L21: +0.33+0.33; peak L21: +0.45+0.45). Across 55 probe seeds the trans-layer mean is +0.191+0.191 and the peak is +0.449+0.449 at L21 with zero variance to four decimal places; context-bootstrap 95%95\% CI [+0.184,+0.196][+0.184,+0.196]; all 77 jackknife gaps in the interval [+0.095,+0.250][+0.095,+0.250] (strictly positive).

3.4 Mistral-7B (7.24B parameters)

Five legal-license + placeholder sequences screen at log⁡P/tok>−1.0\log P/\text{tok}>-1.0 on base Mistral-7B-v0.1 [32] (no fine-tuning). LOO yields trans-layer mean gap +0.30+0.30 (peak L11: +0.47+0.47); four of five sequences contribute positively (cluster-specific). Stable across 5 probe seeds (seed-to-seed std <0.001<\!0.001). Full per-sequence and heatmap results: Appendix C.

Finding 3.

On Mistral-7B (7.24B), LOO cross-sequence probing across 55 naturally memorized sequences yields a true–pure gap of +0.30+0.30 averaged across transformer layers (peak +0.47+0.47 at L11). The signature emerges by mid-network, replicating the Pythia-70M and GPT-2 medium pattern at ∼20×\sim\!20\times the parameter count of GPT-2 medium. Stable across 5 probe seeds (seed-to-seed std <0.001<\!0.001).

Finding 4.

Mistral-7B multi-seed stability: 55 probe random states all give the same +0.471+0.471 peak gap at L11 to 44 decimal places; the trans-layer mean of +0.355+0.355 (seed-to-seed std <0.001<\!0.001) replicates GPT-2 medium’s zero-variance pattern. Layer-position invariance with cluster-specific behaviour holds at ∼21×\sim\!21\times GPT-2 medium parameter count.

3.5 The Probe Direction is Causally Separable from Recall

The signature exists (Findings 1–4); a sharper question is whether the direction the probe reads is itself load-bearing for recall. We answer this with a direct intervention: extract the LOO probe direction at the peak-gap layer and surgically project it out of the residual stream.

Protocol.

On base Pythia-70M with the same 7 naturally memorized sequences, fit a single logistic-regression probe at the peak-gap layer L4 (no LOO for this step – we use all 7 sequences for the strongest-possible direction). Let w^\hat{w} be the unit-normalized probe weight vector in the original residual-stream basis (post-destandardization). Install a forward hook on transformer block 3 (whose output produces hidden_states[4]) that projects w^\hat{w} out of the residual:

h′=h−(h⋅w^)​w^h^{\prime}=h-(h\cdot\hat{w})\,\hat{w}

The hook applies to every token position and every subsequent forward pass while installed. Re-run the full LOO protocol with the hook active and measure per-sequence log⁡P/tok\log P/\text{tok} on both the memorized sequences and an 8-sentence held-out set.

Result 1: gap collapses locally, reconstitutes downstream.

At the intervention site (L4), projecting out the probe direction flips the gap from +0.44+0.44 (memorized activations clearly distinguishable) to −0.19-0.19 (memorized activations indistinguishable or anti-correlated with the probe direction). This collapse tells us that at L4, the probe direction is the primary readout vector for the memorization signature in that layer. Yet crucially, the signature is not localized to L4: downstream layers (L5, L6) spontaneously reconstitute the signature even though they receive modified inputs. This reveals that residual-stream information about memorization is distributed and redundant: projecting a single direction at a single layer does not permanently erase it, because downstream layers can locally recompute or re-encode the signature from partial upstream information. The geometry of memorization in pretrained models is not a sparse, superposition-like encoding but a thick, multi-depth phenomenon.

Table 2 reports the per-depth memorization-specific gap before and after the intervention.

Result 2: behavioural recall is largely preserved.

Per-sequence log-probability drops are small: MIT +0.04+0.04 nats, Apache +0.08+0.08, GPL +0.08+0.08, BSD +0.12+0.12, python_main +0.10+0.10, creative_commons +0.12+0.12, lorem_ipsum +0.19+0.19 (mean drop +0.105+0.105 nats/token). Held-out log-probability on 8 unrelated natural sentences is essentially unchanged (−5.013→−4.990-5.013\to-4.990 nats/token, a decrease of 0.0230.023 in surprisal, i.e., a slight improvement). The intervention does not damage general capability and only minimally damages memorization recall, despite collapsing the probe-measured signature at the intervention site.

Interpretation.

This is the mechanistic bridge between the paper’s two halves. The toy-model story (Sections 4–5) shows that head-level behavioural suppression leaves within-sequence probes saturated at 1.0001.000. The pretrained-model story (Sections 3.2–3.4) shows that cross-sequence LOO signatures exist at scale, distinct from behavioural recall. This section closes the loop: at Pythia-70M scale, the probe-measured signature and the recall mechanism are separable in a direct intervention. You can remove the signature at its locus and leave recall nearly intact, because downstream layers reconstruct whatever signature is needed or route memorization through other channels. The implication: a probe that reads 1.0001.000 accuracy does not imply the probed direction is load-bearing for the behaviour. And conversely, a behaviourally unlearned model may still leak a probe-readable signature through other layers, because the probe and the behaviour are not pinned to the same direction.

Finding 5.

On Pythia-70M, projecting the fitted L4 probe direction out of the residual collapses the cross-sequence gap +→−0.19+0.44\!\to\!-0.19 at the hook layer with full downstream reconstitution by L6, while memorized recall drops by ≤0.19\leq 0.19 nats and held-out capability is unchanged. Probe-readable structure and recall-producing structure are separable directions.

Residual-stream steering: quantitative supplement.

As a complementary measurement that the probe direction is locally readable but not load-bearing for the recall pathway, we add α​w^\alpha\hat{w} at the peak-gap layer L4 and sweep α\alpha, comparing against a random unit-vector control r^\hat{r} (cos⁡(w^,r^)=0.0487\cos(\hat{w},\hat{r})=0.0487). Single seed, single architecture (Pythia-70M), 7 naturally memorized sequences. Per Table 3, subtractive steering along w^\hat{w} and along the random control r^\hat{r} produce comparable recall drops at magnitudes that preserve held-out capability. The probe direction does not produce an outsized recall-suppression effect over the random control, as one would expect if the probe direction were the dominant causal pathway for recall.

3.6 Vocabulary-Matched Probe Control

A potential confound in our LOO protocol is that the separated representational signal might reflect vocabulary-level differences rather than memorization-specific structure. To directly address whether probe accuracy depends on the statistical distinctiveness of the secret tokens themselves, we trained two independent toy models on structurally identical secrets that differ only in their key tokens: (A) the standard secret “The launch code for Project Orion is 88492,” and (B) a matched variant with an arbitrary placeholder “The launch code for Project XKQVZ is 73916.” Both tokens (XKQVZ, 73916) are character sequences absent from the training corpus, carrying no statistical weight.

Both models reached P⁡(secret)=0.0001P(\text{secret})=0.0001 (matched memorization strength). On the cross-sequence LOO protocol, both reach full probe separability at 1.0001.000 before and after unlearning. Critically, the lexical control (comparing XKQVZ/73916 vs. XKQVZ/29481 with identical prefix but different completion) also yields probe accuracy 1.0001.000, directly ruling out a pure token-identity explanation: the signal reflects memorization-specific structure in the residual stream, not surface properties of the secret tokens.

Finding 6.

On the toy model, the linear probe reaches 1.0001.000 for a vocabulary-matched secret where the key tokens are arbitrary character sequences, and for a within-variant lexical control (identical prefix, different completion). Token distinctiveness is not the driver of the probe signal. The separated representation reflects memorization-specific encoding at the head-input level, not surface characteristics of the secret tokens.

3.7 Robustness Analyses of the Cross-Sequence Signature

To ensure the cross-sequence LOO signature is not an artifact of probe initialization, context sampling, or sequence selection, we characterize variance under three independent robustness conditions: probe-initialization stability, neutral-context resampling (bootstrap), and sequence jackknife.

Probe initialization stability.

We refit the LOO pipeline five times with different random seeds ({0,1,2,42,99}\{0,1,2,42,99\}) holding all data fixed. On GPT-2 medium, the transformer-layer mean gap is +0.191+0.191 with a five-seed min-max envelope of width zero (to four decimal places), and the peak gap at L21 is +0.449+0.449 (5-seed std <0.0001<\!0.0001). The probe converges to the same global optimum regardless of initialization, indicating the found direction reflects genuine structural signal rather than algorithmic or stochastic noise.

Context resampling (bootstrap).

We resample the neutral-context pool with replacement for 100 bootstrap replicates while holding the probe seed fixed. The 95%95\% confidence interval for the transformer-layer mean gap on GPT-2 medium is [+0.184,+0.196][+0.184,+0.196] (width 0.0120.012), and for the peak gap is [+0.440,+0.473][+0.440,+0.473] (width 0.0330.033). Zero lies far outside the CI at every depth from L12 onward, providing strong evidence the signature is not context-dependent noise.

Sequence jackknife.

We drop one of the seven screened memorized sequences from both training and evaluation, rerunning the LOO pipeline seven times. All seven leave-one-sequence-out gaps remain strictly positive (range [+0.095,+0.250][+0.095,+0.250]), with the overall effect driven by multiple sequences rather than any single one. The effect survives removal of the largest single contributor (bsd_license, dropping it reduces the trans-layer gap to +0.095+0.095 but does not eliminate it).

Finding 7.

The cross-sequence LOO signature on GPT-2 medium is robust to three independent variance sources: (i) probe-initialization variance is zero to four decimal places across five seeds; (ii) context resampling yields a 95%95\% CI of [+0.184,+0.196][+0.184,+0.196] for the mean gap, excluding zero; and (iii) no single memorized sequence drives the effect. The signature reflects genuine structural signal rather than algorithmic artifact or sequence-specific idiosyncrasy.

4 Methodological Warm-Up: Mechanistic Toy Verification

To answer mechanistically why head-level unlearning fails to collapse the probe (Section 3), we use a controlled toy transformer where causal attribution is unambiguous. This setting also surfaces the saturation problem the LOO protocol corrects: single-sequence probes reach 1.0001.000 by construction (Section 3.1). Findings here are toy-specific; cross-architecture claims are the LOO results in Section 3.

4.1 Problem Formulation

Let ℳθ\mathcal{M}_{\theta} be a Transformer having memorized secret SS such that Pθ​(S∣prefix​(S))>τP_{\theta}(S\mid\text{prefix}(S))>\tau (τ=0.90\tau=0.90). Our goal is to produce ℳθ′\mathcal{M}_{\theta^{\prime}} satisfying:

Pθ′​(S∣prefix​(S))\displaystyle P_{\theta^{\prime}}(S\mid\text{prefix}(S)) <ϵb(behavioural erasure)\displaystyle<\epsilon_{b}\quad\text{(behavioural erasure)} (1)
Acc​(probe on ​Zℋ)\displaystyle\text{Acc}(\text{probe on }Z_{\mathcal{H}}) ≈0.5(representational erasure — desired but not guaranteed)\displaystyle\approx 0.5\quad\text{(representational erasure --- desired but not guaranteed)} (2)
PPLθ′​(𝒟clean)\displaystyle\text{PPL}_{\theta^{\prime}}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}}) ≈PPLθ(𝒟clean)(capability preservation)\displaystyle\approx\text{PPL}_{\theta}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}})\quad\text{(capability preservation)} (3)

where Zℋ∈ℝdheadZ_{\mathcal{H}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}} denotes the mean-pooled output activation vector of the target attention head, and h(l)h^{(l)} denotes the residual stream at layer ll. We distinguish these when analyzing representational content at different computational depths.

4.2 Key Design Principle

MLDU’s split-objective formulation serves two distinct purposes: (1) The 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} recall-suppression objective achieves behavioural erasure by disrupting the value-routing mechanism responsible for secret recall. (2) The 𝐖q/𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{q}/\mathbf{W}_{k} MMD objective simultaneously probes whether attention-pattern disruption can achieve representational erasure. Our ablation (Table 6) shows that 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}-only achieves complete behavioural erasure (P=3.5×10−6P=3.5\times 10^{-6}), while adding the QK component does not reduce it further and, crucially, does not reduce probe accuracy. The central toy-model finding is therefore not about the efficiency of the split objective — it is about the ceiling of what any head-level intervention can achieve under the single-sequence probe: all conditions, including aggressive QK distribution-matching, leave linear probe accuracy at 1.0001.000. In the toy setting, the separation between storage and expression is not a design choice but an architectural property that determines the fundamental limit of head-level unlearning under this probe protocol. The separate cross-sequence signature at scale is treated in Sections 3.2–3.4.

4.3 Method Overview

The pipeline has three phases. Phase 1 (memorization baseline): train a 4-layer, 8-head Transformer [33] (810,496 parameters, character-level tokenization, injection density 16.67%) until P⁡(S∣prefix)=1.000P(S\mid\text{prefix})=1.000 and held-out PPL =1.39=1.39 (Appendix E). Phase 2 (causal tracing): for each head (l,h)(l,h), cache the post-attention head output z^(l,h)\hat{z}^{(l,h)} on a clean prompt (containing the secret trigger) and patch it into a corrupted run (non-trigger entity substituted), then compute:

NCE​(l,h)=Ppatch(l,h)−PcorruptPclean−Pcorrupt\text{NCE}(l,h)=\frac{P_{\text{patch}}^{(l,h)}-P_{\text{corrupt}}}{P_{\text{clean}}-P_{\text{corrupt}}} (4)

Heads with NCE​(l,h)≥δ\text{NCE}(l,h)\geq\delta form ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}. NCE values are not additive; the profile characterizes functional concentration. Phase 3 (split-objective unlearning): freeze all parameters except 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q}, 𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k}, 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} of heads in ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}; apply two independent optimizers (full pseudocode: Algorithm 1 in Appendix E):

Update ​𝐖q,𝐖k:\displaystyle\text{Update }\mathbf{W}_{q},\mathbf{W}_{k}: ℒQ​K=ℒLM+γ⋅MMD2​(Zℋsecret,Zℋclean)\displaystyle\quad\mathcal{L}_{QK}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\gamma\cdot\text{MMD}^{2}(Z_{\mathcal{H}}^{\text{secret}},Z_{\mathcal{H}}^{\text{clean}}) (5)
Update ​𝐖v:\displaystyle\text{Update }\mathbf{W}_{v}: ℒV=ℒLM+α⋅ℒrecall\displaystyle\quad\mathcal{L}_{V}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{recall}} (6)

This decomposition aligns optimization objectives with functional roles, eliminating the gradient interference observed in joint optimization (see Appendix I). MMD [34] bandwidth uses the median heuristic with five scales. The constructive extension MLDU-E (probe-geometry alignment, PGA) and its scaling validation across four architectures are detailed in Appendix P.

5 The Behavioural–Representational Dissociation

Conceptual setup: two possible worlds.

The central claim of this section is that behavioral suppression and representational erasure are mechanistically separable. The null hypothesis would be the opposite: if unlearning disrupts the information flow that produces recall, then it must also disrupt the representations that carry it — no dissociation, tight coupling. Under that view, a model that no longer generates the secret should also show no linearly separable signature in its residuals. But this paper demonstrates that the hypothesis is false. A toy transformer’s output can be surgically silenced at a single attention head (dropping P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret}) to 10−410^{-4}) while internal representations at upstream residual streams retain full linear separability. The mechanism responsible for reading and routing memorized information (the head being modified) is distinct from the mechanism responsible for encoding it (the residual-stream geometry). Unlearning the former does not automatically unlearn the latter.

5.1 Setup and toy-model headline result

We evaluate the pipeline of Section 4.3 on a 4-layer toy transformer (810,496 parameters, vocab=43, seq_len=64) trained to memorize “The launch code for Project Orion is 88492” at injection density 16.67%. Phase 2 causal tracing across all 32 heads identifies a single dominant head L0H7 with NCE =1.000=1.000 [35]; Phase 3 applies the split objective at ℋtarget={(L0,H7)}\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}=\{(\text{L0,H7})\}. Full architecture, training, and dynamics: Appendix E, N.

The unlearned toy achieves P⁡(S)=0.0001P(S)=0.0001 at PPL =1.40=1.40 (+1.2%+1.2\%), modifying only 6,1446{,}144 of 810,496810{,}496 parameters (0.76%0.76\%). The single-sequence linear probe at the target head retains accuracy =1.000=1.000 — the within-model dissociation finding.

5.2 Statement

Finding 8.

On the controlled toy transformer, behavioural unlearning applied at a localized retrieval head (L0H7) suppresses recall (P⁡(S∣prefix)P(S\mid\text{prefix}) drops to 10−410^{-4}) while a linear probe trained on matched-prefix decoys on the residual stream ZℋZ_{\mathcal{H}} remains at accuracy 1.0001.000. Under the embedding-level sensitivity control (Section 5.7) the same probe collapses to chance, so the persistence reflects a surviving representational signal rather than probe insensitivity.

Storage vs. expression on the toy model.

Our toy-model results suggest a local separation between storage and expression: the secret-discriminative signal visible at ZℋZ_{\mathcal{H}} is read and routed to the output by L0H7. Unlearning L0H7 disrupts expression without modifying the upstream encoding under the tested method. We emphasize this is a toy-model claim under a fixed probe protocol; the broader cross-sequence signature at scale is addressed separately (Sections 3.3, 3.4).

This behaviour persists across every toy-model unlearning objective tested (Appendix I), including MLP-only and joint (attention++MLP) interventions (Section 5.10). Projection removal experiments further show the signal is redistributed rather than erased under these head-level interventions.

5.3 Sub-Head Evidence and Ablation

Table 6 isolates each component. 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}-only recall suppression achieves complete behavioural erasure (P=3.5×10−6P=3.5\times 10^{-6}, PPL =1.18=1.18); 𝐖q/𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{q}/\mathbf{W}_{k}-only MMD changes attention patterns but leaves P⁡(secret)=0.9996P(\text{secret})=0.9996. The full split objective and 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}-only both leave the probe at 1.0001.000: the ceiling is structural, not an effort artefact.

5.4 Probe Validity and Causal Locus

Two controls establish the probe is measuring memorization rather than token-level artefacts or a correlated feature. First, a matched-prefix decoy (...Orion is 88492 vs. ...Orion is 12345) shares tokens up to the completion position; under this protocol the probe still reads 1.0001.000 on both original and unlearned models (full table, Appendix 5.7). Second, zeroing the residual stream at successive depths collapses both recall and probe accuracy: embedding-level zeroing drops P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret}) from 0.99990.9999 to 0.00370.0037 (99.6%99.6\% reduction) and collapses the probe from 0.9820.982 to chance (Condition B, Section 5.7).

Finding 9.

On the toy transformer, the embedding-level residual carries a large fraction of the causally relevant signal for secret recall: zeroing it reduces P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret}) by 99.6% and collapses the probe to chance. The probed separability and the recall-producing signal are causally linked in this controlled setting.

Finding 10.

On the toy transformer, interventions restricted to L0H7’s weight matrices suppress behavioural recall without collapsing the linear probe. Representational erasure under this probe protocol requires modifying parameters at or before the residual stream depth where the recall-critical signal first appears.

Cross-architecture replication.

The toy-model dissociation reproduces at 7070M and 345345M parameters when the MLDU pipeline (NCE tracing + split-objective update) is applied to a fine-tuning-injected secret on Pythia-70M (logP:−→−5.72\log P\!:{-0.019}\!\to\!{-5.72}, matched-decoy probe stays at 1.0001.000 at all 77 depths; Finding 18) and to a naturally memorized sequence on GPT-2 medium (Apache License 2.0 preamble, logP:−→−11.74\log P\!:{-0.116}\!\to\!{-11.74}, |ℋtarget|=57|\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}|=57 heads, matched-decoy probe stays at 1.0001.000; Finding 19). Full numbers: Appendix L.

5.5 Natural vs. Injected Memorization: A Probe-Level Distinction

Sections 3.2–3.4 establish a cross-sequence signature for naturally memorized content. A separate question is whether this signature also characterizes content that was memorized by rapid fine-tuning injection (as in Section 3.2 and much of the toy-model work).

Protocol.

We inject a target secret (‘‘The launch code for Project Orion is 88492’’) into Pythia-70M via fine-tuning with early stopping when log⁡P⁡(target)/tok>−0.3\log P(\text{target})/\text{tok}>-0.3. The natural-memorization pool is screened on the base Pythia-70M before fine-tuning; we verify after fine-tuning that all natural-memorized sequences survive (log⁡P/tok\log P/\text{tok} within 11 nat of base).

We then fit a LOO probe using the natural-memorization pool as training data (per Section 3.1) and evaluate it on the injected target and its matched decoy. The probe is asked: “Does the target secret lie on the memorized side of the hyperplane trained on natural memorization?”

Result.

Across the six transformer-layer depths, LOO-target accuracy averages ≈0.50\approx 0.50 in both the memorized and the post-unlearning models. The probe trained on natural memorization does not distinguish the injected target from its decoy.

Interpretation.

This is a null result for the transfer claim but a positive result for the distinction claim. The natural-memorization signature at 70M scale does not generalize to rapidly-injected verbatim secrets, even when both are present in the same model. The two regimes produce mechanistically distinct linear-probe signatures.

Extended test: multi-secret injection (R3B).

To control for the possibility that the negative transfer result reflects only the dissimilarity of 1 injected secret to 4 licenses, we additionally inject 5 secrets simultaneously (Orion, Apollo, Sigma, Delta, Kappa) with matched-prefix decoys, then LOO across the 5 secrets. The pure-distinguishability baseline (0.700.70) is higher than the memorized-class LOO (0.440.44): the matched decoys for injected secrets (which differ only in the last few tokens) produce a distinguishability pattern that the probe reads more reliably than any memorization signal the 5 secrets share. We interpret this as: rapid fine-tuning does not build a cross-secret linear structure in Pythia-70M that a probe can latch onto, distinct from the structure that would exist for any 5 arbitrary distinct sequences. This reinforces the natural-vs-injected distinction.

Finding 11.

In Pythia-70M, a cross-sequence probe trained on naturally memorized sequences does not recognize fine-tuning-injected secrets. Natural pretraining memorization and rapid fine-tuning memorization produce distinct linear-probe signatures in the residual stream.

5.6 Multi-Secret Robustness of the Dissociation

To ensure the toy-model behavioural–representational dissociation is not an artifact of a single memorized secret, we ran the full MLDU pipeline independently on 8 secrets spanning 5 structural types: numeric codes, alphanumeric tokens, a proper name, a date, and a location phrase. Each secret received its own freshly initialized model, tokenizer, causal tracing run, and unlearning pass — no components are shared across secrets. This addresses a natural concern that the key finding (probe =1.000=1.000 after behavioural erasure) might reflect an idiosyncrasy of the primary secret “88492.”

Across all 8 secrets, we observe consistent qualitative behaviour: causal localization is concentrated (NCE ≥0.40\geq 0.40 for all), behavioural unlearning succeeds for secrets with |ℋtarget|≥9|\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}|\geq 9, and probe accuracy remains at 1.0001.000 in every case. Table 7 reports per-secret outcomes; Figure 5 summarizes the results.

Representational retention is universal.

Even the 3 behavioural failures show probe accuracy =1.000=1.000. Representational retention holds regardless of secret type, circuit size, or whether behavioural erasure succeeded. This decoupling — probe=1.000=1.000 in all 8 cases while behavioural outcomes vary — directly strengthens Finding 8: the internal representation of the secret is preserved by the architecture upstream of any head-level intervention, independent of what the unlearning optimizer achieves at the output level.

Behavioural erasure correlates with circuit size.

The 4 cases where P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret}) did not drop below 0.050.05 all have |ℋtarget|≤5|\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}|\leq 5, while all 4 successes have |ℋtarget|≥9|\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}|\geq 9. This clean separation suggests that when causal responsibility is highly concentrated (few heads), the gradient signal from the unlearning objective is too weak relative to the frozen model’s prior to suppress the secret within the fixed optimization budget. Secrets with larger |ℋtarget||\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}| appear easier to suppress under a fixed optimization budget; this is an empirical observation rather than a fundamental limitation of MLDU.

Finding 12.

Across all 8 secrets, linear probe accuracy remains at 1.0001.000 after unlearning, regardless of secret type or behavioural outcome. The behavioural–representational dissociation is not an artifact of a single example; representational retention is universal and independent of whether behavioural erasure succeeds.

5.7 Lexical Identity Control: Full Results

To rule out a pure token-identity explanation for the linear probe signal, we test whether the probe relies on surface lexical properties of the secret tokens or on memorization-specific representational structure. We compare three probe conditions on the same toy model with matched-prefix decoy pairs: (i) standard, comparing the full secret against clean completions from a different prefix; (ii) lexical control, comparing the secret to a decoy that shares the same prefix and context structure but differs only in the memorized completion; and (iii) prefix-only, testing whether the prefix alone permits discrimination.

Finding 13.

Across all three toy-model conditions, the linear probe reaches 1.0001.000 in both original and unlearned regimes. Notably, the lexical control (same prefix, different completion) yields full separability, ruling out a pure token-distinctiveness hypothesis. The retained signal reflects memorization-specific representational structure, not surface characteristics of the secret tokens.

5.8 Embedding Intervention Control: Probe Sensitivity Verification

A natural objection to the dissociation claim is that the linear probe might trivially read 1.0001.000 regardless of the intervention applied, rendering it an unreliable indicator of representational content. To validate probe sensitivity, we test whether the probe can detect actual representational erasure when it is genuinely achieved, across five conditions on the toy model.

Protocol.

All conditions use the matched-prefix decoy comparison (PREFIX + secret vs. PREFIX + random 5-digit decoy), which controls for sequence length and prefix identity. We test: (A) MLDU head-level intervention, (B) embedding zeroing (upstream), (C) 50×50\times embedding noise injection, (D) null ablation of a random head, and (E) original baseline. We measure both behavioural erasure (P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret})) and representational retention (probe accuracy on ZℋZ_{\mathcal{H}}).

The critical comparison is Conditions A vs. B: both achieve P⁡(secret)≈0P(\text{secret})\approx 0, but only B reduces probe accuracy to chance (0.500). Embedding zeroing, which operates upstream of all head-level operations, collapses the probe; head-level unlearning (A), null ablation (D), and even 50×50\times noise injection (C) leave the probe saturated at 0.982. This dissociation is not a consequence of the optimization algorithm but reflects the structural locus of the memorization signal: upstream of all head-level interventions in this toy model.

Finding 14.

The linear probe is sensitive to actual representational erasure in the toy setting: zeroing the token embeddings collapses probe accuracy from 0.982 to 0.500 (chance level). Head-level unlearning, null head ablation, and noise injection all leave the probe at 0.982, confirming that the toy-model probe is not trivially saturated. The dissociation claim is robust: the probe specifically fails to detect erasure under head-level interventions because those interventions do not erase the upstream encoding in this model.

5.9 Mechanistic View: Attention Pattern Disruption

To provide parameter-level mechanistic evidence of how head-level unlearning operates, we directly visualize the attention patterns of the recall-causal head (L0H7) before and after MLDU. The visualization provides a concrete view of the routing disruption that underlies the dissociation: while the upstream encoding survives, the downstream routing of that signal to the output is modified.

Protocol and result.

We extract and visualize the attention weights of L0H7 on the secret prefix (“The launch code for Project Orion is 88492”) at initialization, after unlearning, and compute the difference map. Before unlearning, L0H7 concentrates attention on the final secret token positions (total weight 0.394 at prediction time). After MLDU, this concentration is redistributed (0.319), a reduction of 7.5 percentage points. The difference map shows a clear blue region at the secret token positions, indicating decreased attention.

Critically, the attention patterns of the seven non-target heads are virtually unchanged before and after unlearning, confirming surgical specificity: only L0H7’s routing pattern is modified. The routing-disruption is partial rather than total, consistent with the split-objective design where 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} is the primary suppression mechanism and the ℒQ​K\mathcal{L}_{QK} term acts as secondary attention-pattern smoothing. The probe stays at 1.0001.000 because the upstream token embeddings that L0H7 reads from are unchanged — only downstream routing is modified.

Finding 15.

MLDU disrupts the routing function of L0H7 without eliminating it: the head’s total attention weight to secret token positions decreases from 39.4% to 31.9% after unlearning. This partial disruption is consistent with 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} being the primary suppression mechanism (preventing value-weighted aggregation from reaching the output), while the query-key routing pattern is only partially modified. The parametric view confirms that head-level unlearning operates strictly downstream of where the memorization signal is stored.

5.10 Intervention Breadth and Representation Geometry

The dissociation observed in our main experiments might be specific to attention head interventions. We test this by applying the same recall-suppression objective to three alternative intervention loci: MLP layers, the joint combination of attention and MLP, and the embedding table itself. All experiments use identical toy models, hyperparameters (α=50\alpha=50, η=5×10−4\eta=5\times 10^{-4}, 150 epochs maximum), and the same probe protocol measured on L0H7 activations (ZℋZ_{\mathcal{H}}).

Breadth result.

Despite the breadth of intervention locations ranging from attention heads through MLPs to embeddings, all sites achieve behavioural erasure (P⁡(secret)≈0P(\text{secret})\approx 0) yet leave the linear probe at 1.0001.000 in the toy setting. This remarkable invariance suggests the dissociation is a structural property of the toy probe protocol and the toy model’s architecture, not a head-level artifact. The separable signal appears encoded redundantly across multiple residual stream pathways, resistant to localized removal.

Representation geometry: projection removal.

To understand why downstream interventions fail to collapse the probe, we extract the probe’s weight vector w^\hat{w} on the original model and surgically remove this direction from all activations: z′=z−(z⋅w^)​w^z^{\prime}=z-(z\cdot\hat{w})\hat{w}. On the original model, projection removal reduces probe accuracy from 1.0001.000 to 0.8330.833, confirming the direction captures meaningful signal. However, on the unlearned model (under any intervention), projection removal has no effect: probe accuracy remains 1.0001.000. This reveals that unlearning does not erase the signal but reorganizes the representation such that it becomes resistant to projection-based removal. The representation geometry becomes more robust, not less, after intervention.

Finding 16.

The behavioural–representational dissociation holds across all tested intervention sites: MLP layers, joint attention+MLP, and even the embedding table. This breadth-of-locus invariance implies the dissociation is a structural property of the model and probing setup, not specific to attention heads. Furthermore, projection removal reveals that unlearning reorganizes rather than erases the representation: the separable signal becomes distributed across directions, more resistant to targeted removal after unlearning than before.

6 Comparison with Existing Unlearning Methods

We evaluate five additional methods on the same toy and the same probe protocol, spanning the three families of Ren et al. [21]: divergence-driven (GA, NPO [16], SimNPO), representation-misalignment (RMU), and rejection-based (IDK [5]). Headline: MLDU also fails the probe. MLDU modifies only the causally-identified heads (|ℋtarget|≤12|\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}|\leq 12, <1%<\!1\% of parameters) — the best case for precision-based unlearning. That MLDU leaves the probe at 1.0001.000 alongside NPO, SimNPO, RMU, and IDK argues the dissociation is not a tuning artefact but a structural property of where unlearning objectives operate relative to where the memorization signal lives.

RMU — the only method designed to misdirect internal representations — still leaves probe =1.000=1.000 at PPL =403.3=403.3. NPO and SimNPO [36] achieve strong behavioural erasure (P=0.000P\!=\!0.000, PPL 4.84.8/3.93.9) yet still leave probe at ceiling. The toy probe ceiling reflects that each method operates downstream of where the toy signal lives (Finding 9); the constructive answer (PGA) appears in Section 7. The per-method bar chart is in Appendix H.

7 Probe-Geometry Alignment (PGA)

The cross-sequence signature replicates across four scales (Section 3), raising a constructive question: can a surgical intervention erase the signature itself, not merely suppress behavioural recall? We answer this affirmatively with probe-geometry alignment (PGA). This section gives the headline result; full method derivation, four-method failure analysis, robustness checks, and ablations are in Appendix P.

7.1 Method

Refit the cross-sequence linear probe on the current model’s activations every KK training steps. Extract its unit-norm weight vector w^d\hat{w}_{d} at each residual depth dd. Train with

LPGA​(θ)=CEclean​(Mθ)⏟capability+λ​∑d=0D∑c,i(w^d⊤​[hd,θ​(c+Pisec)−hd,θ​(c+Picln)]pos=plen−1)2.L_{\mathrm{PGA}}(\theta)=\underbrace{\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{clean}}(M_{\theta})}_{\text{capability}}+\lambda\sum_{d=0}^{D}\sum_{c,i}\Bigl(\hat{w}_{d}^{\top}\bigl[h_{d,\theta}(c+P^{\mathrm{sec}}_{i})-h_{d,\theta}(c+P^{\mathrm{cln}}_{i})\bigr]_{\mathrm{pos}=p_{\mathrm{len}}-1}\Bigr)^{2}. (7)

The alignment term is one scalar per depth (the projection along the probe’s own readout direction), not the dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}-dim L2 of feature-matching distillation [10]. This distinction is the source of PGA’s novelty against DANN [12] (full-residual gradient reversal), LEACE [11] (closed-form linear projection at inference), and AAE (isotropic alignment).

Provable property.

If LPGA→0L_{\mathrm{PGA}}\to 0 at every depth and w^d\hat{w}_{d} is the maximum-information linear probe direction, then linear separability of mem vs. clean classes along w^d\hat{w}_{d} goes to zero, and probe accuracy is upper-bounded by the majority-class baseline (Appendix P.2).

Why a 1-D constraint suffices.

The probe reads a single direction: w^d⊤​hd​(x)\hat{w}_{d}^{\top}h_{d}(x). Aligning the full residual over-constrains the optimization relative to what the probe actually uses. PGA’s scalar penalty acts only on the readout direction, while AAE’s full-residual L2 acts on all dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} directions. Empirically, PGA achieves deeper probe collapse (0.650.65 vs 0.700.70 toy max; below-chance only under PGA) at comparable PPL (Appendix P.2).

Intuition: constraint geometry must match readout geometry.

The core insight is that the erasure constraint should have the same dimensionality as the detection constraint. A linear probe’s sole degree of freedom is which direction to read. If the memorization signature lives (at least in part) along that direction, we need to move activations orthogonal to it to suppress the signature. Constraining all dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} directions (as in feature distillation or full-residual alignment) is both more restrictive and less targeted: it forces the model to match some global similarity metric to a reference at the cost of general capability, even though the probe only cares about one scalar. PGA’s rank-one constraint per depth is the minimal surgical incision: push activations off the probe’s readout line while leaving all other directions free. This asymmetry is what permits below-chance probe collapse without significant PPL cost.

Coverage matters: CLPA ablation.

Aligning only at the 33/3232 NCE-localized heads (CLPA) suppresses recall to ×10−52.5\!\times\!10^{-5} but leaves the cross-sequence probe at 0.840.84: the probe reads from all heads, so the 33 recall-causal ones are insufficient coverage (Appendix P.5).

Failure modes that motivate PGA.

Before presenting PGA, we examine why three other surgical families fail on the cross-sequence toy (Table 11). MEMIT suppresses recall 99.99%99.99\% but leaves the probe at 1.001.00 (output-level illusion); multi-depth projection collapses the probe only at ×5.8\!\times PPL cost (capability wall); clean-teacher distillation matches outputs but not activations (representation-level illusion). PGA is the only approach that simultaneously suppresses recall, drives the probe below random chance at deep depths, and preserves PPL. Full per-method analysis: Appendix P.1.

7.2 Cross-architecture results

PGA successfully drives the probe below chance at all four scales. Table 12 and Figure 7 report results. GPT-2 medium required a method variant (MD-PGA, k=2k\!=\!2 eigenbasis) to reach 0.0610.061 at L21 due to sample undersampling (Appendix P.7). Six adversarial probe variants (different seeds, regularizations, nonlinear MLPs) remain within the 0.720.72 ceiling at memorization-relevant depths (Appendix P.6).

MD-PGA: eigenbasis variant for under-determined regimes.

On GPT-2 medium (N=≪dmodel=1024N\!=\!84\!\ll\!d_{\mathrm{model}}\!=\!1024), the LR-coef direction is under-determined and PGA plateaus at 0.7260.726. Replacing it with the top-kk eigenvectors of the standardised between-class scatter Sd=(μm,d−μc,d)​(μm,d−μc,d)⊤+(Σm,d−Σc,d)S_{d}=(\mu_{m,d}\!-\!\mu_{c,d})(\mu_{m,d}\!-\!\mu_{c,d})^{\top}+(\Sigma_{m,d}\!-\!\Sigma_{c,d}) — Multi-Depth PGA (MD-PGA) — drives the probe to 0.061\mathbf{0.061} at k=2k\!=\!2, L21, 0.130.13 nats recall cost (Appendix P.7). The eigenbasis is the optimal rank-kk covariance separator; the LR coef ignores the second-order structure that matters when N≪dmodelN\!\ll\!d_{\mathrm{model}}.

Finding 17.

Probe-geometry alignment (PGA) collapses the cross-sequence LOO probe below the 0.50.5 random baseline at memorization-relevant layers on toy (d4:0.17d_{4}:0.17), Pythia-70M (d5,6:0.07d_{5,6}:0.07), and Mistral-7B (d24,28:0.45d_{24,28}:0.45), and GPT-2 medium (L​21:0.061L21:0.061 with MD-PGA k=2k\!=\!2, 0.130.13 nats recall cost). The collapse is robust to six adversarial probe variants at memorization- relevant depths. PGA drives cross-sequence probe accuracy below random chance in a controlled setting; its mechanism (1-D alignment along the live probe readout direction) differs from feature-matching distillation, gradient-reversal adversarial alignment, and closed-form linear projection.

7.3 Robustness against probe-shopping

A natural objection: PGA is trained against a specific linear probe; an adversary may fit a different probe and recover memorization. We test this directly with six adversarial probe variants (4 logistic regressions across seeds and L2 strengths; 2 MLPs) on the PGA-edited toy and Pythia-70M models. Worst-case max probe at memorization- relevant layers stays within the 0.720.72 floor target (0.660.66 on toy, 0.710.71 on Pythia-70M L2–L6). L0–L1 violations on Pythia (0.790.79) are predicted token-identity leakage, not signature recovery. Full per-variant matrices: Appendix P.6.

7.4 PGA variants and Pareto-frontier analysis

Beyond the headline LR-coef and MD-PGA recipes used for the cross- architecture results, we ran four diagnostic experiments that probe the design space of PGA: scaling (MD-PGA on GPT-2 medium), iterative extensions (Adaptive PGA), per-head fusion with MLDU’s localization (CA-PGA), and robustness against re-fitting attackers (Adversarial PGA). Each variant was motivated by a specific limitation uncovered during development. LR-PGA plateaued on large-dimensional problems (GPT-2 medium), motivating MD-PGA. Single-direction projection seemed crude, motivating iterated extensions (Adaptive). The signature appeared distributed, motivating a per-head variant (CA-PGA). And the fixed probe seemed vulnerable, motivating an adversarial procedure (Adversarial PGA). Each is a self-contained notebook in the release; we summarise the headline finding and the regime/limitation motivating each below.

MD-PGA: closing the GPT-2 medium gap (sample-starved regime).

The original LR-direction PGA on GPT-2 medium plateaus at probe 0.7260.726 (layer 16) due to the under-constrained gradient signal at N≪dmodelN\ll d_{\mathrm{model}} — a common regime in deployment where we have few memorized examples relative to model width. We resolve this with Multi-Depth PGA (MD-PGA): instead of training PGA along the LR probe’s coef direction, construct the rank-kk null projector from the top-kk eigenvectors of the standardised between-class scatter Sd=(μm,d−μc,d)​(μm,d−μc,d)⊤+(Σm,d−Σc,d)S_{d}=(\mu_{m,d}-\mu_{c,d})(\mu_{m,d}-\mu_{c,d})^{\top}+(\Sigma_{m,d}-\Sigma_{c,d}) at the target depth dd. With k=2k\!=\!2 at L21 alone, MD-PGA drives the probe from 1.0001.000 to 0.0610.061 (well below chance) with 0.130.13 nats recall cost on the Apache License preamble (data: gpt2m_md_pga_results.json). The eigenvector basis is the optimal rank-kk direction for separating mem vs clean covariance, unlike the LR coef direction which is the optimal single linear separator and ignores covariance structure. The completed scaling story: PGA’s mechanism transfers across architectures; the projection direction must be chosen from the between-class scatter eigenbasis when the probe-coef direction is under-determined (N≪dmodelN\ll d_{\mathrm{model}}).

Adaptive PGA: why rank-1 is near-optimal (diminishing returns regime).

One might expect that projecting multiple directions (higher rank) would erase the signature more thoroughly. We tested two iterative variants to explore this: vanilla iteration (refit probe and project the new direction at each round) and recall-aware iteration (project only the recall-orthogonal component, with a smart stop on probe-at-target ≤0.55\leq 0.55 or recall budget exceeded). The motivation was to understand whether the signature is fully 1-D or whether there are recall- orthogonal components worth targeting. On Pythia-70M, both confirm the rank-1 design sits at a near-optimal point on the erasure-vs-capability Pareto frontier: the recall-aware variant self-terminates at rank-11 in 5/65/6 depths (notebook mldu_e_adaptive_pga_v2.ipynb), while vanilla iteration to rank-1010 degrades capability (Δ​log⁡P=−1.82\Delta\log P\!=\!-1.82 nats vs. rank-11’s −1.20-1.20 nats) with only marginal erasure gain. Beyond rank-11, the cross-sequence signature has no recall-orthogonal directions left to project — additional rank only damages the recall mechanism without further erasing the signature, providing a methodological justification for the paper’s headline single-direction design.

CA-PGA: why signatures are distributed (robustness to surgical localization).

A natural hypothesis from MLDU’s head-level localization was that recall and the cross-sequence signature might be concentrated in the same heads. If true, a per-head rank-11 PGA applied only to the top-kk causally-relevant heads would suffice, saving computation. We tested this fusion (CA-PGA) to understand the distribution of memorization structure. On Pythia-70M with k=3k\!=\!3 heads per layer (Fig. 25; data: mldu_e_causally_aware_pga_results.json), the per-head heatmap shows nearly uniform per-head probe accuracy (0.850.85–1.01.0) across all 88 heads at L2–L6 — the cross-sequence signature is distributed across heads, not concentrated. Surgical per-head projection accordingly fails to erase (0.920.92–0.960.96 post-CA-PGA vs. 0.710.71–0.810.81 post-PGA), although it preserves recall ×3\!\times better (−0.37-0.37 vs. −1.20-1.20 nats). This validates the paper’s separation of concerns: MLDU uses head-level NCE localization for behavioural recall (which IS concentrated in a few heads), and PGA uses full-residual projection for the cross-sequence signature (which is distributed).

Adversarial PGA: defeats re-fit attackers (adaptive-attacker threat model).

The §7.3 probe-shopping test fixes the adversary’s probe family in advance. A stronger and more realistic threat model is a re-fitting attacker with white-box access who trains their own linear probe directly on PGA-treated activations: such an attacker recovers ∼0.70{\sim}0.70 LOO accuracy at L3–L6 on Pythia-70M even after MD-PGA k=3k\!=\!3 (where the original construction-aligned probe collapses to 0.070.07). This gap motivated a more robust variant. We tested adversarial PGA: initialize UkU_{k} with the LR-coef direction and iteratively (i) re-fit a probe on PGA-treated activations and (ii) augment UkU_{k} with the orthogonal component of the new probe direction (Gram–Schmidt). This iterative adversarial procedure matches the attacker’s learning loop and attempts to preemptively erase any new directions they might find. On Pythia-70M with 2424 mem ++ 2424 clean license/prose prefix pairs, adversarial PGA reaches rank-66 and defeats the re-fit probe at all six mem-relevant depths (max post-PGA accuracy 0.520.52, all <0.65<\!0.65). Counter-intuitively the recall cost is lower than naive MD-PGA k=3k\!=\!3 (−0.39-0.39 vs. −4.46-4.46 nats on the Apache License preamble) and CKA preservation against the representational-similarity detector of Xu et al. [2] is higher (CKA ≥0.95\geq 0.95 at 4/64/6 depths vs. 0/60/6 for MD-PGA k=3k\!=\!3, with deep-layer CKA reaching 0.990.99 at L3–L4 vs. 0.130.13 under naive MD-PGA). The mechanism is direction targeting: adversarial search finds low-variance probe-discriminative directions, whereas Σdiff\Sigma_{\mathrm{diff}} eigenvectors over-erase high-variance representation that is not probe-relevant. Per-fold MD-PGA k=3k\!=\!3 (one projector per LOO fold, paper-aligned protocol) does not suffice on its own — a re-fit probe still recovers 0.550.55–0.870.87 accuracy — because the per-fold protocol only excludes the test sequence from PGA fitting and does not change the rank or direction-search method. We tested four PGA variants head-to-head (Fig. 24; data: mldu_e_pga_upgrades_comparison_results.json); only the adversarial variant defeats the re-fit probe at every depth while preserving recall.

Capability preservation: deep-layer restriction matters.

We further benchmark adversarial PGA on five zero-shot capability tasks from lm-evaluation-harness (HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ, ARC-Easy, WinoGrande). Applying adversarial PGA at all six layers L1–L6 (rank-66) damages BoolQ by −9.4-9.4pp (mean Δ​acc=−0.024\Delta\mathrm{acc}=-0.024 across the five tasks), revealing that shallow layers carry reading-comprehension structure orthogonal to the cross-sequence signature. Restricting adversarial PGA to deep layers L4–L6 only converges in 44 iterations at rank-44 (max post-PGA LOO probe 0.480.48, well below the 0.550.55 target) and preserves all five benchmarks: per-task |Δ​acc|≤2.8|\Delta\mathrm{acc}|\leq 2.8pp, mean Δ​acc=+0.2\Delta\mathrm{acc}=+0.2pp, BoolQ specifically +2.8+2.8pp (Fig. 8; data: mldu_e_capability_benchmarks_adversarial.json). The deep-layer restriction is not optional: it is required for the capability-preservation claim to hold. Combined with the re-fit-attacker defeat established above, deep-layer adversarial PGA satisfies the joint criterion of (i) collapse against a re-fitting attacker probe, (ii) preserved recall on the construction prompt, and (iii) preserved zero-shot capability across five standard benchmarks. This positions adversarial PGA as a robustness extension when the deployed PGA must withstand attackers who re-fit probes against the released model.

8 Discussion and Conclusion

What we show.

While concurrent attacks demonstrate that behavioural unlearning is not robust, we go further by localizing where retained content lives: in a cross-sequence linear signature for naturally memorized content in mid-network residual streams. The signature generalizes via LOO across three architectures, is distinct from string features, shows cluster-specificity to formal-register text, and is causally separable from the recall mechanism (§3.5). Crucially, a probe trained on natural memorization does not classify fine-tuning-injected secrets (Section 5.5), revealing that the two regimes produce representationally distinct traces — suggesting unlearning claims need finer stratification by regime.

What this changes for unlearning evaluation.

Current practice in unlearning evaluation is almost entirely behavioral: does the model still generate the target secret? This paper shows that answer is insufficient. A model that passes behavioral evaluation (“forgets” on standard benchmarks) can still harbor linearly separable signatures in its internal activations, and these signatures persist across architectures and scales. The implication for evaluation protocols is concrete: joint behavioral plus representational acceptance criteria are necessary. Specifically, we propose that unlearning claims should require both (1) behavioral suppression (target generation probability <ϵbehav<\epsilon_{\text{behav}}, typically 10−310^{-3} in the literature) and (2) representational erasure (cross-sequence probing accuracy ≤0.5\leq 0.5 at memorization-relevant depths, plus robustness to six adversarial probe variants). Behavioral-only acceptance will continue to give a false sense of security. Representational-only acceptance (in isolation) is impractical, since representations are distributed and probing is not deployable at inference time; but as an evaluation criterion for research and before release, it is essential.

MLDU-E and practical implications.

Four surgical method families fail in distinct ways (weight editing, multi-depth projection, output distillation, full-residual L2); probe-geometry alignment (PGA) targets the scalar along the probe’s readout direction at each depth and collapses the signature below random chance at toy (→0.651.00\!\to\!0.65), Pythia-70M (→0.070.93\!\to\!0.07), Mistral-7B mid-layers (0.450.45), and GPT-2 medium via the MD-PGA k=2k\!=\!2 variant (→0.0611.00\!\to\!0.061 at L21 with 0.130.13 nats recall cost). The guiding principle — erasure constraint geometry must match probe read geometry — generalizes across four orders of magnitude (Appendix P). Practically: the rank-one-per-depth constraint appears to sit at a near-optimal point on the erasure-versus-capability frontier, as shown by iterative extensions that self-terminate at rank-one (Adaptive PGA). Applied thoughtfully across multiple scales, PGA offers a scalable surgical approach.

8.1 Limitations

Controlled setting and scale.

Our primary mechanistic analysis is conducted on a 4-layer character-level transformer trained on a synthetic task — a simplified setting that enables precise causal localization. We mitigate the scale concern through two replication experiments (Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium) that both replicate the dissociation at natural memorization. However, evaluation at larger scales (Llama-class, GPT-4-scale) remains important, as memorization may be more distributed and circuit structure more complex in those models.

Localization assumptions.

MLDU depends on identifying a target circuit via causal tracing. In the toy setting, a single dominant head suffices. In larger models, causal responsibility may be distributed and attribution less precise. While our GPT-2 work shows MLDU can handle multi-head targets, effectiveness in highly distributed settings remains uncharacterized.

Token-level confounds in synthetic data.

In the synthetic setup, secret and clean prompts differ at the token level, contributing to embedding-space separability. Although lexical-identity controls eliminate differences at the completion position, embedding-level signals may still correlate with continuations. Our findings establish that linearly separable representations persist, but do not fully disentangle whether these arise from memorization-specific encoding or token-level statistics.

Three pieces of evidence mitigate this concern. First, the toy lexical-identity control (Section 5) with constant prefix entities rules out prefix-token identity as the sole driver. Second, the cross-sequence LOO protocol on pretrained models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, Mistral-7B) reports memorization gaps above pure-distinguishability baselines (Findings 1, 2, Finding 3) — this is the primary evidence that cross-architecture memorization structure is not explained by string-level features alone. Third, the per-sequence LOO tables in Appendix D and Appendix C show the cluster-specific pattern directly: the signature generalizes within formal-register English (licenses, web prose) but not to code or placeholder text, indicating that the cross-sequence structure cannot be reduced to vocabulary overlap. A fully controlled experiment with vocabulary-matched secret and background texts remains an important direction for future work.

Single-seed and limited variability analysis.

All experiments are conducted with a fixed random seed. While results are consistent across multiple independently trained models with different secrets, we do not quantify variability across seeds for a given setup. Future work should evaluate the stability of causal localization, unlearning dynamics, and probe measurements under different initializations.

Scope of representational analysis.

We focus on linear separability as a criterion for representational retention, measured via probes on head activations and residual stream representations. While linear probes provide a strong and interpretable signal, they capture only one aspect of representation geometry. It is possible that other forms of structure (e.g., nonlinear or distributed encodings) behave differently under unlearning. Extending this analysis to richer representational metrics is an open direction.

Interpretation of behavioural failures.

In the multi-secret experiment, behavioural unlearning does not succeed for all secrets within the fixed optimization budget, and success correlates with circuit size. While this suggests that distributed circuits may be more amenable to suppression, we do not establish a causal relationship, as optimization hyperparameters are not varied. Further work is needed to understand how circuit structure interacts with unlearning dynamics.

Implications for real-world privacy.

Our findings highlight a potential gap between behavioural unlearning and representational retention, but we do not demonstrate a direct attack that exploits these retained representations. The practical privacy risk depends on whether such internal signals can be extracted or leveraged in realistic threat models. Establishing this connection is an important direction for future research.

8.2 Future Work

Multi-seed and robustness analyses across architectures.

We performed multi-seed probe characterization (5 probe random states) on all three pretrained architectures: Pythia-70M (Section 3.2, Finding 1), GPT-2 medium (Finding 2; +0.191±0.000+0.191\pm 0.000 trans-layer mean gap), and Mistral-7B (Finding 4; mid-layer gap +0.355+0.355, peak +0.471+0.471 (both with 5-seed std <0.001<\!0.001)). On GPT-2 medium we additionally report context-pool bootstrap 95% CIs and sequence jackknife (Appendix 3.7). Extending bootstrap and jackknife protocols to Pythia-70M and Mistral-7B remains future work; random-initialization null controls at GPT-2-medium and Mistral-7B scale would tighten the “learned property of pretraining” claim. This variability quantification is important for downstream work that relies on the cross-sequence signature as a target.

Extending probe-direction intervention to larger models (core mechanistic question).

We performed a direct probe-direction intervention on Pythia-70M (Section 3.5, Finding 5): fitting the LOO probe at the peak-gap layer, extracting its weight vector w^\hat{w}, and projecting w^\hat{w} out of the residual stream via a forward hook. The result on Pythia is informative: the gap collapses locally (+0.44→−0.19+0.44\to-0.19 at the hook layer) but is reconstituted downstream, while per-sequence log-probability is essentially unchanged. Running this intervention on GPT-2 medium and Mistral-7B would reveal whether the downstream-reconstitution pattern is architecture-general or scale-dependent. This is arguably the most important mechanistic experiment remaining, as it directly characterizes whether memorization in larger models exhibits the same storage-versus-expression separation observed in the toy. A finding that downstream reconstitution is universal would suggest that distributed memorization across scales fundamentally separates encoding from routing. A finding that the pattern breaks at scale would indicate qualitative differences in how larger models organize memorized information.

Downstream extraction attacks: bridge representational leakage to practical privacy risk.

This paper demonstrates that internal representations leak memorized content to white-box probes, but does not establish that this leakage is practically exploitable. The missing link is an end-to-end extraction attack: given a model with a retained cross-sequence signature (as measured by our probes), can an adversary extract the secret using only inference-time access, without direct access to residual streams? Experiments might include (i) membership inference attacks targeting residual-stream similarity; (ii) prompt optimization or prefix-search procedures that indirectly manipulate internal representations toward memorized patterns; (iii) fine-tuning with auxiliary objectives that extract from the signature. Establishing this bridge would move the representational leakage from a theoretical concern to a concrete threat, justifying mandatory representational evaluation.

Richer representational probing.

We use linear and MLP probes, which agree throughout, confirming linear separability. However, deeper MLP probes, kernel methods, or contrastive probing techniques may reveal additional structure in how memorized information is encoded. Extending the representational analysis to nonlinear manifolds would strengthen the claim that the signature is not an artefact of probe capacity.

Relearning resistance by intervention locus.

We observe that the unlearned model requires 5×5\times more steps to recover the secret than the original. This resistance has not been characterised as a function of intervention site (𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}, MLP, or embedding) or intensity. A systematic comparison of relearning dynamics across intervention types would clarify which approach provides the strongest practical privacy guarantee.

Larger models and alternative architectures.

We test on a 4-layer toy model, Pythia-70M (70M, GPT-NeoX), GPT-2 medium (345M), and Mistral-7B (7.24B). Whether the cross-sequence signature and cluster-specificity pattern hold in larger decoder-only models (e.g., Llama-70B, GPT-4-scale), in encoder-decoder architectures, or in mixture-of-experts models remains an open question. The two-orders-of-magnitude replication presented here suggests robustness, but empirical validation at the largest scales is an important direction.

Downstream extraction attacks.

We demonstrate that head-level unlearning on the toy model leaves linearly separable representations accessible to white-box probes. Whether an adversary with model access can translate this retained representation into a practical extraction attack — through prompting strategies, prefix optimization, or membership inference — has not been tested. Establishing this link would directly quantify the privacy risk of behavioural unlearning without representational erasure.

Representation geometry under unlearning.

Our projection removal experiment shows that unlearning reorganizes rather than erases the secret representation in the toy model. A full principal component or manifold analysis of how the representation geometry evolves during unlearning would clarify whether the signal is rotated, redistributed across directions, or compressed into a lower-dimensional subspace — each with different implications for the difficulty of future erasure attempts.

Appendix A Extended Background and Related Work

This appendix expands §2 with a fuller discussion of the four research currents our work draws on and contributes to: machine unlearning for language models, mechanistic interpretability of memorisation, linear-probing methodology, and concurrent attacks on unlearned models.

A.1 Machine unlearning for language models

Machine unlearning was originally formalised in the privacy literature [13] as the problem of removing the influence of a specific training example from a trained model without retraining from scratch. The classical approach — exact unlearning via SISA-style data partitioning [37] — is impractical for large language models because the partition would have to be re-trained from frozen sub-models. The dominant LLM strategy is therefore approximate unlearning, which targets the model’s output distribution on the forget set while attempting to preserve everything else.

Approximate methods cluster into four families. (i) Gradient-ascent methods maximise the model’s loss on forget sequences — pure gradient ascent (GA) is unstable and capability- destructive, leading to refinements such as preference-based negative optimisation NPO [16] and SimNPO, which add a reference-model regulariser. (ii) Localised parameter editing rewrites the weights of a specific MLP or attention layer [25, 26]; these methods change a single factual association at a time and are not designed for sequence-level unlearning. (iii) Distillation-based methods (e.g. character-level redaction [15]) train a fresh student on a sanitised teacher; they target outputs but are computationally expensive. (iv) Selection-based methods (RMU [7], IDK-style refusal training) replace the forget content with a default refusal or random vector at the activation level. Comprehensive surveys [17, 21] catalogue dozens of variants in each family.

The dominant evaluation framework, TOFU [5], scores whether the unlearned model still generates the target sequence verbatim or produces a refusal. MUSE [6], WMDP [7], and KnowUnDo extend this with multi-task and harm-specific axes. All of these benchmarks are behavioural: they query the model’s output distribution, not its internal state.

A.2 Why behavioural success can hide representational retention

The gap between behavioural removal and representational removal has been recognised across several literatures. Geva et al. [38] and follow-up work [25, 26] show that factual associations are stored in mid-network MLP layers in distributed form: the same fact can be triggered by many semantically related prompts, suggesting that an output-level edit can leave the underlying storage intact. Turner et al. [27] and the activation-engineering line demonstrate that targeted vector additions at intermediate layers can re-elicit suppressed behaviours, again pointing to representational content that survives output suppression. Nasr et al. [9] showed that adversarial prompting can extract memorised content from production-scale models even when straightforward generation does not reveal it. Each of these results is consistent with the picture that a behaviourally clean model can still encode the unlearned content; none of them locates the encoding directly.

A complementary line of work uses linear probes to ask what a hidden state knows about a label [23, 24, 28]. Probe accuracy lower-bounds the linear information present in a representation: if a linear probe can classify post-unlearning activations, the relevant structure is still linearly readable. Probes have been used to detect concept information [11], syntactic structure [24], and truthfulness but they have not been used as a primary criterion for whether unlearning has reached the internal storage — this is the niche our work targets.

A.3 Causal localisation and circuit-level analysis

To intervene on storage rather than output, one needs to know where in the network the storage lives. Causal tracing [25] estimates each component’s causal contribution to a target token by patching activations between a clean and a corrupted run, identifying a small set of MLP layers as the “factual association” locus. Component-level path patching [35] and circuit analyses [28] extend this to attention heads and to multi-step computations. We use causal tracing to localise the head most responsible for secret retrieval in our toy transformer; this lets us test whether MLDU’s head-level intervention actually reaches the storage the probe reads from, rather than only silencing the output.

A.4 Concurrent attacks on unlearning

A growing body of recent work demonstrates, by exhibiting attacks, that approximate unlearning suppresses rather than removes content. Hu et al. [3] show that a small amount of benign downstream fine-tuning recovers most of the “forgotten” content (relearning attack). Zhang et al. [4] show that post-hoc weight quantisation alone — with no further training — partially restores forgotten outputs (quantisation attack). Jia et al. [20] show that behavioural unlearning fails to generalise to paraphrased or semantically adjacent prompts, suggesting the underlying knowledge is intact. Meta-analyses [18, 19, 21, 22] reach similar conclusions across method families.

The two papers most directly comparable to ours both characterise internal traces of unlearning. Chen et al. [1] extract spectral fingerprints from principal activation directions of the unlearned model and use them to classify model identity (i.e., to recognise that a given model has been subjected to unlearning) with high accuracy — a model-level rather than sequence-level signature. Xu et al. [2] quantify representational drift of an unlearned model relative to its pre-unlearning checkpoint via PCA, CKA, and Fisher information, taxonomising reversibility based on the geometry of that drift. Both works infer retention by comparing models across versions (pre- vs. post-unlearning); neither asks whether a held-out memorised sequence is recognisable from activations of a single fixed model.

A.5 Our contributions in context

Against this backdrop our four contributions sit at distinct slots in the literature. (i) Our cross-sequence LOO probe (§3.1) is the first probing protocol we are aware of that asks whether a memorisation signature generalises across sequences within a single fixed model — a stronger criterion than spectral fingerprinting (which is per-model) or representational drift (which requires the pre-unlearning baseline). (ii) Our causal-separability result (§3.5) closes a gap left by activation- steering work: prior work shows steering can re-elicit content; ours shows the probe direction can be projected out without damaging recall, which means the probe-readable structure and the recall- producing structure occupy genuinely separable subspaces. (iii) The regime distinction (§5.5) between naturally pretrained memorisation and rapid fine-tuning-injected secrets bears on the external validity of toy/synthetic unlearning experiments: a probe that classifies one regime does not transfer to the other. (iv) The constructive method PGA (§7) closes the loop — not just detecting retention but eliminating it — positioning the work alongside concept-erasure methods (LEACE [11], INLP), feature-matching distillation [10], and gradient-reversal alignment [12], distinguished by aligning along the live-updated probe direction in 1-D rather than dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}-D.

The combined picture: behavioural metrics are insufficient acceptance criteria for unlearning; cross-sequence linear probes provide a direct representational test; the structure they detect is causally separable from the recall mechanism and surgically removable; and the removal generalises across four orders of magnitude of model scale.

Appendix C Mistral-7B: Per-Sequence LOO Results

The heatmap (Figure 10) reveals the cluster-specific structure of the cross-sequence signature: formal-register English and licenses contribute strongly, while code and pseudo-Latin sequences contribute near-chance, on Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, and Mistral-7B alike.

Table 14 reports per-sequence leave-one-out accuracy on Mistral-7B, averaged across mid-layer depths (L3–L10) where the signature is strongest. Four of the five screened sequences (the legal-license cluster) contribute strongly to the cross-sequence signature, with per-sequence LOO well above the pure baseline. The placeholder sequence lorem_ipsum sits just above the pure baseline, consistent with the cluster-specificity pattern reported on GPT-2 medium: the signature generalizes within formal-register English text but not across structurally dissimilar clusters. The bsd_license sequence contributes positively but less strongly than the other legal licenses (0.740.74 vs. 0.940.94–1.001.00).

Appendix D GPT-2 Medium: Per-Sequence LOO Results

This appendix supports Section 3.3 (Finding 2) with seed-by-seed and per-sequence LOO detail on GPT-2 medium. Figure 11 shows the five-seed panel; the visual identity across seeds reflects logistic-regression convergence to the same global optimum given the training-fold size.

Table 15 reports per-sequence leave-one-out accuracy on GPT-2 medium at L12 (the depth of sharp signature onset) and L21 (the depth of peak gap). At L12 the cluster-specific pattern is clean: four legal-license sequences and one web-prose sequence reach LOO ≥0.96\geq 0.96, while code and placeholder sequences sit at chance. At L21 all seven sequences reach or approach ceiling — including, interestingly, python_main and lorem_ipsum, both of which sit at 0.500.50 at L12. The strong cluster-specificity claim is carried by L12; by the final layers the separability becomes less cluster-bound, as the probe (trained on a single depth) latches onto per-sequence features that emerge late. This pattern is consistent with Finding 2.

Appendix F Probe Experimental Details

White-box probes (T12) were trained on Zℋ∈ℝ16Z_{\mathcal{H}}\in\mathbb{R}^{16} (mean-pooled L0H7 output) using 150 secret and 150 clean samples, 70/30 stratified split. The MLP probe uses hidden layers (64, 32), ReLU activations, and early stopping. The linear probe uses ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized logistic regression. Both probes were trained on held-out samples not seen during unlearning. We repeated the experiment across 5 random train/test splits; all 5 runs returned 1.000 accuracy for both probe types. The agreement between linear and MLP probes confirms linear separability, ruling out overfitting.

Appendix G Relearning Experiment Details

Relearning (T13): AdamW, LR=10−3=10^{-3}, batch size 1, secret-only training. Original model recovers at step 1; unlearned model at step 5. The 5×5\times difference reflects disruption of the output routing circuit (𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}). We do not claim strong relearning resistance; the absolute values remain low.
