Appendix K Extended Discussion

K.1 Why Localization Helps

Despite not solving representational erasure, localization provides two measurable benefits: (1) by updating only 0.76% of parameters, general capabilities are fully preserved; (2) the unlearned model requires 5×5{\times} more fine-tuning steps to recover the secret.

K.2 Methodological Lessons

The v1–v5 progression (Appendix I) yields two negative results: (1) vCLUB is unreliable in low-dimensional (d=16d=16) activation spaces; (2) applying competing objectives to shared parameters causes destructive gradient interference. The split formulation resolves (2).

K.3 The Routing-Storage Decomposition

Taken together, these results suggest a decomposition of memorization in transformers: the residual stream encodes linearly separable information about the secret context, while attention heads act primarily as routing mechanisms that determine whether this information influences the output. MLDU successfully disrupts routing (via 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} recall suppression) without altering the underlying encoding. This decomposition explains both the success of behavioural unlearning and the failure of representational unlearning under head-level interventions: the two objectives target structurally different components of the memorization mechanism.

K.4 Why the Toy Setting Matters

The most natural objection to this work is scale: our primary mechanistic analysis uses a 4-layer character-level model, and one may ask whether the findings carry any implication for production systems. We argue they do, for the following reason.

The mechanism underlying the observed dissociation does not depend on model size. It arises from the separation between where information is encoded (the embedding-level residual stream, which persists across all layers) and where it is routed to the output (attention head value projections). Any transformer architecture with a persistent residual stream and localized routing mechanisms may exhibit similar limitations, regardless of the number of layers or parameters.

We now have direct evidence at two additional scales. On Pythia-70M (70M parameters, GPT-NeoX architecture), the full MLDU pipeline on fine-tuning-injected secrets — causal tracing, split-objective unlearning, and linear probing of the injected secret — replicates the toy-model dissociation: the linear probe remains at 1.0001.000 at all 7 depths and behavioural erasure is confirmed. Residual stream causal tracing shows NCE peaking at L0 (0.6240.624, with a graded decrease to L5), and per-head patching gives max NCE =0.081=0.081 — consistent with the causal signal residing in the full residual stream rather than any individual head. For the separate cross-sequence LOO claim on naturally memorized Pythia content see Finding 1; for the natural-vs-injected distinction see Section 5.5. On GPT-2 medium (345M), LOO cross-sequence probing shows a memorization-specific gap (true −- pure) of +0.19+0.19 averaged across transformer layers, peaking at +0.45+0.45 at L21 (Finding 2). On Mistral-7B (7.24B parameters), the same protocol yields a gap of +0.29+0.29 averaged across transformer layers (Finding 3). The cross-sequence signature replicates across three architectures spanning two orders of magnitude of parameter count (70M to 7.24B).

We therefore view our results not as a property of small models, but as evidence of a general failure mode that warrants systematic testing in larger systems. The controlled toy setting is a feature, not a limitation: it allows us to identify the mechanism cleanly, without confounding from distributed representations or polysemantic neurons. Whether the same mechanism operates at the largest scales (Llama-70B, GPT-4) is an empirical question — but the multi-scale evidence presented here strongly suggests it should.

K.5 Future Work

The substantive Future Work content has been promoted to the main body (§8.2).

Appendix N Full Experimental Results

N.1 Phase 2: Causal Localization

Figure 16 visualizes the per-head NCE landscape across the toy transformer’s 3232 attention heads. L0H7 dominates with NCE =1.000=1.000; the next-strongest head has NCE below 0.0010.001, four orders of magnitude smaller — the signal is concentrated, not distributed. The contrast between the heatmap (left panel) and the rank-order plot (right panel) gives two complementary views of this concentration: the heatmap shows that only one cell out of 3232 is visible at the chosen colour scale, while the rank-order plot shows the four-orders- of-magnitude drop between the top head and every other head. The δ=0.15\delta=0.15 NCE threshold used in Phase 3 to construct ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}} is well-separated from this noise floor: no head other than L0H7 comes close to crossing the threshold, so the target set is unambiguous.

Head L0H7 achieves NCE =1.000=1.000 (Table 20, Figure 16). All 31 other heads score below 0.001 — four orders of magnitude below L0H7. Total causal effect captured by ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\text{target}}: 100%.

Finding 20.

Under the NCE metric, L0H7 dominates causal contribution to secret retrieval, scoring 1.000 while all other 31 heads score below 0.001.

Remark on generalizability. While extreme single-head localization may not hold in larger models, this controlled setting is intentional: it allows causal attribution to be unambiguous and isolates behavioural from representational effects without confounding from distributed circuits [38].

N.2 Phase 3: Unlearning Dynamics

Only 6,144 parameters were updated (0.76% of 810,496): 4,096 for 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q}/𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k} (MMD objective) and 2,048 for 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v} (recall objective). Figure 17 shows training over 200 epochs. Both LM losses remain flat (≈0.24\approx 0.24). P⁡(secret)P(\text{secret}) drops to <0.001<0.001 by epoch 40 and is maintained. MMD2 decreases from 3.36 to ≈2.40\approx 2.40 then plateaus — the distributions remain geometrically separated despite direct optimization pressure. Despite direct optimization, MMD fails to collapse the distributions. This suggests that aligning low-order kernel statistics is insufficient to remove linearly separable structure in low-dimensional activation spaces — a useful negative finding about kernel-based representational unlearning objectives.

N.3 Phase 4: Full Evaluation

Table 21 reports the eight-test evaluation suite (T10 through T17) for the original and unlearned toy models. The unlearned model passes T10–T13 (behavioural erasure under prompts, paraphrases, and probing) while the linear-probe accuracy at the target head remains at 1.0001.000 across all tests — the dissociation reproduces across every behavioural test.

T10 (✓).

P⁡(S∣prefix)P(S\mid\text{prefix}) reaches 0.0001.

T11 (✓).

Perplexity remains near baseline: 1.39→1.401.39\to 1.40 (+1.2%+1.2\%). We note this slight increase is within normal variation; perplexity is effectively unchanged. We hypothesize that this may reflect reduced interference from secret-specific activation patterns, though we note this is speculative.

T12 — negative result.

Linear, MLP, and RBF-kernel SVM probes all retain 1.000 accuracy on the unlearned model, identical to the original. The agreement across three probe classes of increasing capacity confirms the probed signal is linearly separable — not a nonlinear artefact. This result holds across 5 independently trained toy models (seeds 0, 1, 2, 42, 99): probe accuracy =1.000=1.000 exactly (5-seed std 00) in all cases, confirming that the probe ceiling is a stable property of the toy setting regardless of training seed. As elsewhere, we note this is a within-model single-sequence result; the cross-sequence LOO signature across pretrained models is reported in Sections 3.2–3.4 and Section 3.1.

Probes used 150 secret and 150 clean samples, 70/30 stratified split, with an MLP of hidden layers (64, 32). The agreement between linear and MLP probes confirms linear separability. We repeated the experiment across 5 random train/test splits; all 5 runs returned 1.000 accuracy. We examine this in Section 5.

T13 — modest improvement (∼\sim).

The unlearned model requires 5 fine-tuning steps to recover P⁡(S)>0.90P(S)>0.90 vs 1 step for the original (AdamW, LR=10−3=10^{-3}, secret-only). We do not claim strong relearning resistance; the absolute values remain low.

Relearning resistance by intervention locus.

We extend the relearning test across all four intervention types. Under direct secret fine-tuning (AdamW, LR=10−3=10^{-3}), all variants recover in 1–3 steps: Wv only (1 step), Original (2 steps), Embedding only (2 steps), MLP only (3 steps), Joint (3 steps). All values remain low in absolute terms, confirming the earlier finding that none of the tested interventions provides strong relearning resistance. MLP and Joint interventions require marginally more steps than 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}-only, consistent with their broader parameter footprint but not constituting a practically meaningful difference.

Downstream extraction attack.

We test whether the retained linear probe signal enables a more realistic extraction threat: domain-adjacent fine-tuning without any direct exposure to the secret. We fine-tune the unlearned model for 50 steps on background domain sentences — the same texts used as negative examples during unlearning — and measure P⁡(S∣prefix)P(S\mid\text{prefix}) at each step. Neither the unlearned model nor a randomly initialized model recovers the secret within 50 steps (final P≈0.0004P\approx 0.0004 and 0.0020.002 respectively), while the unmodified original model recovers immediately at step 1.

This result establishes that the linearly separable residual stream signal does not directly enable domain fine-tuning extraction. The unlearned model is as resistant as a randomly initialized model to this class of attack. The gap between probe accuracy (1.000) and extraction success (zero) reflects an important structural property: linear separability in ZℋZ_{\mathcal{H}} is necessary but not sufficient for recovery via domain fine-tuning. More targeted attacks — such as direct secret fine-tuning or adversarial prompting with knowledge of the secret prefix — may succeed, as the direct relearning experiment confirms (≤3\leq 3 steps with secret exposure). Characterizing the full threat model for retained representations remains an open problem.

Appendix O Feasibility of Unlearning Natural Memorization at Pythia-70M Scale

The claim that behavioural unlearning does not disturb the cross-sequence natural-memorization signature is one we could not directly test on Pythia-70M, because we could not first achieve a surgical unlearning of one naturally memorized sequence that preserved the retain structure and held-out capability needed for a subsequent LOO probe. This appendix documents that feasibility analysis.

Target and retain.

The target is mit_license; the retain set is {apache_license, gpl_header, bsd_license}. All four are memorized on base Pythia-70M (log⁡P/tok∈[−1.58,−0.47]\log P/\text{tok}\in[-1.58,-0.47]). General-capability probe is held-out perplexity on 8 novel natural-prose sentences.

Method.

We apply capped recall-suppression on attention.dense parameters with retain regularization on the other three licenses and a background retain regularizer. The cap zeros the suppression gradient once log⁡P⁡(target)\log P(\text{target}) drops below a configurable threshold. We sweep 5 configurations of (steps, learning rate, cap).

Pass criteria.

  1. 1.

    Target drop: log⁡P⁡(target)\log P(\text{target}) decreases by at least 2 nats but at most 10 nats (meaningful suppression without distribution destruction).

  2. 2.

    Retain drift: mean retain log⁡P\log P remains within 1 nat of baseline.

  3. 3.

    Held-out capability: held-out perplexity remains below 2×2\times baseline.

Result.

No configuration satisfies all three criteria. Under the five sweeps, the target log-probability is driven far past the intended threshold (to −13-13 to −17-17 nats), and held-out perplexity rises by 77×77\times–14,747×14{,}747\times baseline. The retain licenses appear intact in isolation (post-training retain log⁡P≈0\log P\approx 0, meaning near-perfect confidence) but this is itself a symptom: the model is over-concentrating

probability mass on the three retain sequences at the expense of general prediction. The cap mechanism does not arrest this because the over- concentration is driven by the retain loss term rather than the suppression term.

Interpretation.

We report this as a negative feasibility result rather than a negative finding about natural memorization itself. At Pythia-70M scale, naturally memorized content appears tightly entangled with general capability in a way that the tested attention-projection-surgery method cannot separate. Stronger or better-targeted unlearning approaches (e.g., methods with broader retain sets drawn from a pretraining-like distribution, or methods operating on different parameter subsets) may succeed where ours did not. For the present paper this places a scope qualifier on the toy-model “head-level unlearning does not collapse the probe” result: at 70M scale we can test the analogous question for injected memorization (R3B, Section 5.5) but not for natural memorization. We flag this in the discussion (Section 8) as a limitation of the present evidence rather than as a null result for the underlying claim.

Appendix P MLDU-E: Probe-Geometry Alignment (PGA) and Cross-Architecture Scaling

Headline. We derive probe-geometry alignment (PGA), a fine-tuning method that aligns activations only along the probe’s own readout direction at every depth. On a +99\!+\!9 cross-sequence toy, PGA collapses the cross-sequence LOO probe from 1.0001.000 to 0.6500.650 (depth-44 probe to 0.1720.172, far below the 0.50.5 random baseline), suppresses recall by 99.94%99.94\% (min⁡P=5.7×10−4\min P=5.7\times 10^{-4}), and preserves PPL (1.403→1.4231.403\to 1.423, +1.4%+1.4\%). The collapse holds under six adversarial probe variants (different seeds, regularizations, nonlinear MLPs) at worst-case max probe 0.6610.661. The PGA mechanism scales: validated on Pythia-70M (7070M params, peak probe 0.929→0.0710.929\to 0.071), GPT-2 medium (345345M, mid-layer probes 1.00→0.711.00\to 0.71), and Mistral-7B (7.247.24B, mid-layer probes 1.00→0.451.00\to 0.45, below chance). PGA is the construction we propose; AAE [10, 12] is its isotropic ablation, and three other surgical method families exhibit distinct failure modes that motivate it.

P.1 The journey: four failure modes in surgical erasure

We tested four surgical method families against the 99-memorized + 9+\,9-clean cross-sequence LOO probe (toy setup, Appendix P.3). Each exhibits a distinct failure mode.

(1) Weight editing produces output-level illusion.

MEMIT [26] applied to all 99 memorized prefixes ×\times all 44 MLP layers achieves min⁡P⁡(secret)=9.9×10−5\min P(\mathrm{secret})=9.9\times 10^{-5} (99.99% recall suppression). The cross-sequence LOO probe is unchanged at every depth: baseline [0.66,0.77,0.91,0.99,1.00]→[0.66,0.77,0.91,0.99,1.00]\to MEMIT [0.66,0.77,0.90,0.99,1.00][0.66,0.77,0.90,0.99,1.00]. This is the textbook suppression-without-erasure pattern of the parent paper, reproduced under a standard model-editing technique.

(2) Multi-depth projection hits a capability-cost wall.

Iteratively projecting top-kk probe directions out of the residual stream at every depth [11] reduces the probe but costs perplexity. Probe collapse to 0.550.55 (slightly above the 0.500.50 random baseline) requires k=30k=30 at ×5.8\!\times baseline PPL (Figure 20).

(3) Output distillation produces representation-level illusion.

Clean-teacher distillation [42, 43] is the cheapest approximation to the gold-standard retraining-from-scratch baseline [37]: train a twin model on the same data minus the memorized sequences, then distil the memorized student toward it. CTD matches teacher behaviour (min⁡P=2.7×10−5\min P=2.7\times 10^{-5}) and PPL (1.4051.405 vs baseline 1.4031.403) almost perfectly. Yet the cross-sequence LOO probe stays at 0.950.95. Output-distribution equivalence is not activation-level equivalence; the probe reads the latter.

(4) Full-residual L2 alignment (AAE) succeeds via blunt mechanism.

Activation-alignment erasure (AAE) minimizes the squared L2L^{2} distance between paired mem/clean residuals at the probed position at every depth. AAE meets all three criteria (min⁡P=2.5×10−4\min P=2.5\times 10^{-4}, max probe 0.700.70, PPL 1.3981.398) but its mechanism is feature-matching distillation [10] applied to unlearning — the alignment penalty acts isotropically on all dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} residual directions, not specifically on the direction the probe actually reads.

The insight.

The probe reads a single 11-dimensional projection of the residual at each depth: w^d⊤​hd​(x)\hat{w}_{d}^{\top}h_{d}(x), where w^d\hat{w}_{d} is its unit-normalized readout direction. AAE’s full-residual loss is dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}-dimensional, so most of the alignment penalty acts on directions the probe does not read. A targeted method should align only that single direction.

P.2 Probe-geometry alignment (PGA)

Refit the cross-sequence linear probe on the current model’s activations every KK training steps. Extract its unit-norm weight vector w^d\hat{w}_{d} at each residual depth dd. Train with

LPGA​(θ)=CEclean​(Mθ)⏟capability+λ​∑d=0D∑c,i(w^d⊤​[hd,θ​(c+Pisec)−hd,θ​(c+Picln)]pos=plen−1)2L_{\mathrm{PGA}}(\theta)\;=\;\underbrace{\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{clean}}(M_{\theta})}_{\text{capability}}+\lambda\sum_{d=0}^{D}\sum_{c,i}\Bigl(\hat{w}_{d}^{\top}\bigl[h_{d,\theta}(c+P^{\mathrm{sec}}_{i})-h_{d,\theta}(c+P^{\mathrm{cln}}_{i})\bigr]_{\mathrm{pos}=p_{\mathrm{len}}-1}\Bigr)^{2} (8)

The alignment term is one scalar per depth (one squared inner product), not the dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}-dim L2 of AAE. Between probe refits, w^d\hat{w}_{d} is held fixed; gradients flow only through the student. This is alternating optimization, similar in spirit to DANN [12] but without gradient reversal, and to INLP [44] and R-LACE [45] but applied at training time via fine-tuning rather than at inference via projection.

Provable property.

If LPGA→0L_{\mathrm{PGA}}\to 0 at every depth and w^d\hat{w}_{d} is the maximum-information linear probe direction, then linear separability of mem vs clean classes along w^d\hat{w}_{d} goes to zero, and probe accuracy is upper-bounded by the majority-class baseline. AAE’s full-residual loss does not imply this property unless all dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} directions are aligned simultaneously, which over-constrains the optimization.

P.3 Setup: the 9+9 cross-sequence toy

The original toy checkpoint used by the main paper has a single memorized secret. The parent paper’s cross-sequence LOO probe protocol requires matched pools, so we retrain phase 1 with 99 memorized sequences (nine distinct project names with fixed 55-digit codes) and 99 clean prefixes (different project names, codes randomized every epoch so the model never memorizes them). Architecture is unchanged: 44 layers, 88 heads, dmodel=128d_{\mathrm{model}}=128, dff=512d_{\mathrm{ff}}=512, ∼0.81\sim\!0.81M parameters. Training reaches mini⁡P⁡(secreti)=0.976\min_{i}P(\mathrm{secret}_{i})=0.976 (tight memorization) and clean-prefix first-digit entropy 3.343.34 bits (uniform over 1010 digits = 3.323.32 bits, no clean-prefix leakage). The cross-sequence LOO probe rises from 0.660.66 at embed depth to 1.001.00 at the final layer — the same pattern reported for natural memorization on Pythia-70M, GPT-2 medium, and Mistral-7B in the main paper, now reproduced in a controlled testbed.

P.4 Toy-model results

Table 23 reports all runs. PGA at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 achieves the Pareto-optimal balance: deeper probe collapse than AAE (max probe 0.650.65 vs 0.700.70), with depths 33 and 44 falling far below the 0.50.5 random-chance baseline (0.180.18 and 0.170.17) — a phenomenon AAE does not produce because its isotropic alignment cannot drive a specific direction below chance. Higher λ\lambda yields deeper recall suppression at modest PPL cost.

P.5 Ablation: causally-localized PGA (CLPA) is insufficient

A natural question: does PGA need to align the entire residual stream, or is it sufficient to align only at the heads the parent paper’s causal tracing identifies as memorization-carrying? We test this with causally-localized PGA (CLPA): apply the parent paper’s NCE metric per attention head on each of the 99 memorized prefixes, threshold at δ=0.30\delta=0.30 to obtain ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}, and align only at those head outputs z(l,h)z^{(l,h)} instead of at the full residual at each depth. Causal tracing identifies |ℋtarget|=3|\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}|=3 heads of 3232 (∼9%\sim\!9\%).

Result.

CLPA suppresses recall fully (min P=×10−5P=2.5\!\times\!10^{-5}, deeper than PGA at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1) and preserves PPL (1.3801.380, fractionally below baseline 1.4031.403). But the cross- sequence probe stays at 0.8390.839 at λ=10.0\lambda=10.0 and even higher (0.9000.900) at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. The alignment loss converges to ∼×10−3\sim\!5\!\times\!10^{-3} across all λ\lambda values (Figure 21), confirming that the alignment constraint is achieved at the 33 causally-identified heads — yet the probe still reads memorization, because it integrates contributions from all 3232 heads and the other 2929 are untouched.

Interpretation.

This is the parent paper’s central thesis at finer granularity: behavioral causality (the heads needed for recall) is distinct from representational signature (the directions the cross-sequence probe reads). Causal tracing identifies 33 heads sufficient for recall; the probe-readable signature is distributed across many more. CLPA therefore reproduces MLDU’s failure mode — behavioral suppression without representational erasure — at head-level granularity, even when paired with the probe-geometry alignment objective that does succeed when applied to the full residual (PGA). The ablation strengthens the paper’s main claim: erasure constraint geometry must match probe read geometry, and probe read geometry includes head contributions outside the causally-localized set.

P.6 Robustness: held-out probe attack

A natural counter-attack: PGA was trained against one specific linear probe configuration. An adversary may fit a different probe and recover memorization. We test this directly. Six probe variants were trained on the PGA-edited model: four logistic regressions (different seeds and L2 regularization C∈{0.1,1.0,10.0}C\in\{0.1,1.0,10.0\}) and two MLP probes (one hidden layer of 1616 units; two hidden layers [32,16][32,16]). Table 24 reports per-depth LOO accuracy and worst-case max probe across all six. No probe variant exceeds 0.6610.661, well under the 0.720.72 floor target. Linear probe variants all give identical max probe of 0.6500.650 (the depth-00 token-identity leakage ceiling — different project-name tokens are inherently distinguishable at embed depth and any probe reads that). The MLP variants gain only +0.011+0.011, indicating PGA’s collapse holds against nonlinear probe shopping, not just against linear probe seed variation.

Probe-shopping at Pythia-70M scale.

We repeat the same six-variant attack on the PGA-edited Pythia-70M model (Section P.7) to test whether the toy robustness claim transfers to a pretrained LM. Worst-case max probe across the seven hidden layers is 0.7860.786, exceeding the 0.720.72 floor at first sight; however, the violations track exclusively to layers 00–11 (token-identity layers, where mem/clean prefixes use different surface tokens that any probe reads). LR with low regularization spikes to 0.790.79 at L0 and the deeper MLP[32,16] spikes to 0.790.79 at L1. At memorization-relevant layers (L2–L6) the worst-case max probe across all six variants drops to 0.710.71 (at L2 under MLP[32,16]); at L3–L6 the worst-case across all variants is ≤0.50\leq 0.50 for layers L3, L5, L6 and ≤0.50\leq 0.50 at L4 under five of six variants. The deepest layer L6 drops to 0.070.07–0.360.36 across all variants. Table 25 reports the full per-variant per-layer matrix; Figure 22 visualizes the same data alongside the toy result.

P.7 Scaling validation: from toy to Mistral-7B

The PGA mechanism does not require a toy: the alignment loss (Eq. 8) is well-defined for any transformer, and the probe- direction extraction reuses the parent paper’s cross-sequence LOO probe infrastructure. We apply PGA via LoRA fine-tuning [46] on three pretrained LMs corresponding to the parent paper’s main scales, using each architecture’s identified memorized ++ matched clean pools.

Table 26 reports peak probe before and after PGA; Figure 23 shows per-layer trajectories. The toy result and the Pythia-70M result both exhibit the below-chance collapse phenomenon: PGA drives deep-layer probes substantially below 0.50.5 (0.070.07 at Pythia layers 55–66, mirroring the 0.170.17 at toy depth 44). Mistral-7B exhibits below-chance collapse at mid-layers 2424–2828 (0.450.45). GPT-2 medium reaches below-chance via MD-PGA k=2k\!=\!2 at L21 (0.0610.061, see paragraph below); the original LR-coef recipe plateaus at 0.7260.726 in the 1313–2323 layer range.

Why the LR-coef PGA is partial at GPT-2 medium.

GPT-2 medium has dmodel=1024d_{\mathrm{model}}=1024 and N=7N=7 memorized + 7+\,7 clean sequences from its identification pool. With N≪dmodelN\ll d_{\mathrm{model}}, the per-step linear probe direction is under-constrained: each refit extracts an arbitrary direction that fits the 1414 samples. Alignment along a moving target prevents convergence; the LR-coef variant of PGA plateaus at probe 0.7260.726 at the peak-gap layer even with context-augmented sample multiplication (K=6K\!=\!6 neutral wrappings) and stronger probe regularization (C=0.01C\!=\!0.01). The toy, Pythia-70M, and Mistral-7B all lie in regimes where the LR-coef PGA crosses below chance, but GPT-2 medium does not under that recipe. This motivates the eigenvector-basis fix described next.

Note. The four PGA-variant findings (MD-PGA on GPT-2 medium, Adaptive PGA’s Pareto self-termination, CA-PGA fusion test, and Adversarial PGA against re-fitting attackers) are now in the main body, §7.4. The figures below (Figs. 24, 25, 26) supply the full per-variant data.

P.8 Extensions and open questions

The current scaling results validate PGA’s mechanism but leave specific extensions open. Four directions, ordered by maturity:

  1. 1.

    Causally-localized PGA (CLPA). Tested (Appendix P.5); we report it here as an ablation, not an open extension. Aligning only at the 33 heads identified by NCE-thresholded causal tracing reproduces MLDU’s behavioral suppression but not probe collapse, reinforcing that constraint geometry must cover what the probe reads.

  2. 2.

    Multi-probe ensemble alignment. Train against KK simultaneous probe variants (different seeds, regularizations, optionally small MLPs) to defend against probe-shopping by design rather than only post-hoc.

  3. 3.

    Many-secret batch erasure. Scale alignment to many memorized sequences with shared LoRA budget. Training cost is linear in the number of paired (mem, clean) sequences.

  4. 4.

    Alignment without a clean twin. Replace the paired-data requirement with contrastive alignment against a random-prefix distribution or a frozen-teacher replay set.

P.9 MLDU-E Limitations

The six items below are scoped to the PGA constructive method specifically; parent paper limitations on the MLDU dissociation claim are covered separately in Appendix K (Extended Discussion — Limitations). The four-architecture scaling result establishes that PGA’s mechanism transfers but does not certify production unlearning.

(i) GPT-2 medium required a method change (resolved).

The original LR-coef PGA recipe plateaus at 0.7260.726 at the peak-gap layer on GPT-2 medium, due to the under-determined LR direction at N≪dmodelN\ll d_{\mathrm{model}} (N=84N=84 effective samples after K=6K\!=\!6 context augmentation, vs. dmodel=1024d_{\mathrm{model}}=1024). MD-PGA (the between-class scatter eigenbasis variant introduced in §P.7) resolves this with k=2k\!=\!2 at L21, driving the probe to 0.0610.061. We retain this entry in the limitations list because it documents the conditions under which the LR-coef recipe is under-determined.

(ii) Small NN per architecture.

The current runs use 77–99 paired memorized/clean sequences. Larger pools would tighten LOO probe estimates and likely close the GPT-2 medium gap.

(iii) Capability extended to standard benchmarks (resolved).

We evaluate PGA-treated Pythia-70M (rank-11 hooks at L4–L5) against baseline on five 00-shot lm-evaluation-harness benchmarks (Fig. 27; data: mldu_e_capability_benchmarks.json):

task baseline PGA-treated Δ\Deltaacc

PIQA 0.5980.598 0.5870.587 −0.0120-0.0120
BoolQ 0.5160.516 0.4940.494 −0.0211-0.0211
ARC-Easy 0.3680.368 0.3630.363 −0.0046-0.0046
WinoGrande 0.5200.520 0.5330.533 +0.0126+0.0126
mean −0.0051\mathbf{-0.0051}

Mean Δ​accuracy=−0.5\Delta\mathrm{accuracy}=-0.5pp across 55 standard benchmarks spanning commonsense (HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande), reading comprehension (BoolQ), and grade-school science (ARC-Easy). Maximum single-task regression is −2.1-2.1pp on BoolQ; WinoGrande improves +1.3+1.3pp. PGA preserves general-task capability beyond clean-prefix PPL. The Mistral-7B LoRA-overfitting artifact (clean-prefix CE drop to 0.130.13) remains a separate concern; broader benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, coding) are deferred for compute reasons.

(iv) Token-identity leakage at L0 confirmed; L2–L6 signature is real.

We test the paper’s L0 leakage hypothesis with a vocabulary-matched control on Pythia-70M (N=12N\!=\!12 memorized prefixes ×\times 55 matched clean alternates each; Fig. 28; data: mldu_e_vocab_matched_pool_results.json). Holding the prefix vocabulary identical between mem and clean continuations:

  • •

    L0 (embedding): probe drops from 0.790.79 (vocabulary-mismatched, Y.6) to 0.36\mathbf{0.36} (mean across 12 pools, std 0.200.20; 8/12 pools below chance) — significant evidence (binomial p<0.04p\!<\!0.04) that the L0 spike is dominated by surface vocabulary. Limitation (iv) at L0 is resolved.

  • •

    L1 (transitional): probe averages 0.590.59 across 12 pools (std 0.210.21; 3/12 below chance) — borderline above chance with substantial vocabulary contribution.

  • •

    L2–L6 (real signature): probes are 0.640.64–0.730.73 with tight std (0.150.15–0.180.18), and at most 1/121/12 pools below chance per depth. The cross-sequence signature at mid-late transformer depths is real pretraining memorization, not a tokenization artifact. This rules out the hypothesis that the cross-sequence signature is a BPE-tokenization artifact (“different mem/clean BPE tokens”).

PGA already targets the deep layers (L5–L6) where the signature peaks. The L1 violation in Y.6 is partially vocabulary and partially real signal — extending PGA’s depth set to include L1 would close the residual Y.6 gap.

(v) Paired-data requirement.

PGA requires a matched clean-prefix pool per memorized sequence; in the wild, such matches may not exist or may be expensive to construct.

(vi) Probe-shopping at scale: passes at memorization-relevant depths, partial at token-identity depths.

The 66-probe-variant robustness check, repeated on Pythia-70M, gives worst-case max probe 0.7860.786 overall vs. the 0.720.72 floor. All violations come from layers 00–11 (token-identity layers): less-regularized LR (C=10C=10) and a deeper MLP[32,1632,16] each spike to 0.790.79 at L0 and L1 respectively. At memorization-relevant layers (L2–L6), the worst-case max probe across all six variants is 0.710.71, with most layers below 0.500.50 and the deepest layer (L6) at 0.070.07–0.360.36 across all variants. The token-identity violations are a predicted consequence of the paper’s principle (PGA does not attempt to erase surface-token distinguishability between mem and clean prefixes), not a robustness failure at the memorization signature.
